Chapter 8: Washington

Congress gave Huang a deadline, the administration reportedly fought with itself over Megaspeed, and the White House stood by him, at least in public.

The House. In a letter dated Wednesday, November 4 and released November 5, three Republican chairs asked Huang to brief their committees, in a closed session, on November 18: John Moolenaar (the Select Committee on China), Brian Mast (Foreign Affairs) and Rick Crawford (Intelligence). It was an invitation, not a summons. The letter said he "must accept the invitation or provide alternative availability by November 11, 2026." ABC asked Mast whether he'd subpoena Huang if he didn't respond. Mast said: "absolutely." On Wednesday, Moolenaar said on Fox Business that Huang "has until the end of the day to respond." TechCrunch reported Moolenaar's view that if he doesn't agree, "he'll likely be subpoenaed." On Wednesday afternoon, per CNBC (published 4:59 PM ET): "Mast and Moolenaar told reporters on Wednesday afternoon that they had not yet heard from Huang and that they were giving him until the end of the day to respond." Asked about a subpoena, Mast said "yes."

The outcome: unknown at 6:35 PM ET. I searched again this evening. I found no report that Huang agreed, proposed another date or declined, and none that a subpoena has issued. The deadline is end of day, so it hadn't technically passed. Here's how it can go:

He agrees, or offers another date. The briefing happens on November 18 or later. Then the question is whether a closed-door session produces anything public.

He doesn't answer. A subpoena is the stated next step. ABC notes the catch: "House Republicans lose control of their committees in January when the chamber turns over to Democrats," so a subpoena issued now would likely lapse.

The board removes him first. Then Congress would be summoning a former CEO, a different and probably less constrained witness.

The Senate. Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) on November 10: "I just think he's got to go." On Wednesday he told CNBC: "As a matter of his own conscience, he should resign." Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.), on Wednesday: "Jensen Huang should resign from Nvidia." Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer aimed at the president instead: "What a dereliction of duty." Sen. Chris Coons, in line to chair Senate Foreign Relations, says Congress will investigate. Sen. Michael Bennet's office released a letter on November 11 to Commerce Secretary Lutnick, Attorney General Blanche, Secretary Rubio and DNI Clayton. It asks, among other things, for an update on the Megaspeed investigation, with answers due "November 24, 2026."

The administration, reportedly divided. On Wednesday, Axios and then CNN reported a confrontation in the White House Situation Room on Thursday, November 5. CNN (people familiar with the matter) says Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pressed Lutnick over why Megaspeed hadn't been put on the Entity List, and "Lutnick did not immediately commit to taking any specific action." CNN's sources say "Commerce has so far refused to put Megaspeed on the entity list," and that senior officials, Lutnick among them, were briefed on the matter months ago. CNN also reports Commerce has added no company to the Entity List in more than a year. The administration denies it. Per a Gizmodo summary, it told both Axios and the NYT that no such confrontation took place. I couldn't read the Axios original (it blocks automated fetching). The CNN text I read is a full syndicated copy. Status: alleged, and officially denied.

Recall the Commerce under secretary from Chapter 6, the official Teter said had given NVIDIA permission to reach out. The NYT reports that Kessler reports directly to Lutnick. Nobody has publicly connected those dots, and I'm not going to. But they're on the same page of the org chart.

The president. Trump has backed Huang personally ("I really believe him"), said the memo "didn't make much of an impact" on him, and said the FBI is looking into "something else." The NYT reports he was briefed on the concern in October 2025.

So Washington is where both cases, spy and not-spy, get argued in public. Here they are, side by side, each at its strongest.

Interior just put selling federal land into its official five-year plan. Before anybody in Washington panics or cheers, look at who actually runs what out here.

Washington has about 12.2 million acres of federal land. Roughly 9.3 million of it is Forest Service, which answers to the Agriculture Department, not Interior. Gifford Pinchot, the Okanogan and the rest of the national forests aren't in this plan as written.

Interior's piece here is about 2.4 million acres. Most of that is national parks, the "nationally significant" kind the plan says Interior will focus on. The BLM share is about 429,000 acres.

The plan names no parcels, no acreage, no prices and no timeline. Republican Ryan Zinke's office says he's "firmly opposed." Democrats take the House in January.

And the most obvious buyer, the state of Washington, is staring at a shortfall Ferguson says runs into the billions.

What to watch:
Interior naming actual parcels
Any land sale bill in Congress
Ferguson's December budget

If Interior offered Washington some BLM ground, would you trust Olympia to keep it open for hunting and grazing?

text:
Battery Storage Is Becoming Critical Infrastructure for AI Data Centers

A new project in Utah offers a practical example of how battery storage is becoming part of the infrastructure behind the AI boom.

Lydian Energy has brought its 150 MW / 600 MWh Faraday Battery Energy Storage System into commercial operation.

The four-hour lithium iron phosphate (LFP) system supports Meta’s Eagle Mountain data center operations and provides contracted storage capacity to PacifiCorp under a long-term agreement.

One detail is particularly important: the battery is located next to an existing 525 MW solar facility and shares its substation and grid connection.

This means the developer can add significant storage capacity without building an entirely new grid connection from scratch.

The broader lesson is that data center power strategies are evolving.

The question is no longer simply where to obtain electricity. It is how to secure reliable capacity, manage peak demand, improve grid flexibility and bring power infrastructure online faster.

For energy developers, this creates opportunities beyond selling battery equipment:

- Long-term capacity and storage agreements
- Solar-plus-storage integration
- Behind-the-meter energy solutions
- Flexible power supply for large industrial customers
- Integrated energy management services

My view: The next phase of the BESS market will be driven increasingly by the value batteries deliver to specific electricity users, not just by installed megawatts or battery prices.

As AI infrastructure expands, storage developers that can combine project development, financing, grid integration and long-term operations will have a competitive advantage.

Source: https://t.co/BnzrwK8rII

#EnergyStorage #BESS #DataCenters #AI #RenewableEnergy #GridFlexibility #EnergyTransition

text:
Virginia just voted on a major constitutional amendment affecting abortion laws. At different points in my life, I've been both pro-life and pro-choice. Here's why I no longer identify with either label:

- When I was pro-life: I avoided thinking about the millions of miscarriages each year. I questioned my religion because I couldn't reconcile the miracle of conception with the cruelty of so many losses. We fight so desperately to save one another that “free will” feels like a cruel explanation. I go to church and send my children to Catholic school, but there are still questions I'm terrified to ask.
- When I was pro-choice: I avoided thinking about where life began to deserve protection. Every line I tried to draw felt arbitrary. I wanted certainty. Instead, I found myself standing in a grayness so vast I hated myself.
- When I was pro-life: I avoided questioning the Church's opposition to IVF. Conception is an almost unimaginable lottery determining who gets to exist. I couldn't understand why helping a loving couple create life through careful, responsible medicine was somehow less sacred. Or how anyone could ask a couple to bury the dreams of children they longed to hold.
- When I was pro-choice: I avoided thinking about premature babies. Parents sitting beside an incubator, watching a machine breathe for someone they already loved beyond reason. Fighting, praying... surviving.
- When I was pro-life: I avoided thinking about the mother of four whose last pregnancy nearly killed her. Now pregnant again, facing the possibility that bringing a fifth child into the world could leave four children without their mother. I could explain the sanctity of the unborn. I couldn't explain away the sanctity of the woman standing in her kitchen, looking at four children who still needed her alive.
- When I was pro-choice: I avoided thinking about the first flicker of cardiac activity. Not yet a fully formed heart, not proof of consciousness, but the beginning of something unmistakably alive and developing.
- When I was pro-life: I avoided thinking about children born into cruelty, only to grow into prisoners we condemn. And I struggled with the hypocrisy of defending their right to be born, only to grow quiet about the suffering that followed. It's why we foster, but our reach is so small.
- When I was pro-choice: I avoided thinking about the abortion itself. Suspended in darkness, defenseless.
- When I was pro-life: I avoided the thought experiment about the burning fertility clinic. A newborn in one room. Several viable embryos in another. Only enough time to save one. I would save the newborn. Yes, I would offer my own life if that somehow made it possible to save them all. But if the choice were absolute, I knew which way I would run. And I hated that my answer left me standing in the grayness again.
- When I was pro-choice: I avoided thinking about Planned Parenthood's history of racism and eugenics. Or the Freakonomics argument that legalizing abortion helped reduce crime. What haunted me was the thought of celebrating a safer world because certain children were never given the chance to live in it.
- When I was pro-life: I avoided imagining a woman in my family being raped and what I would say if she became pregnant. I could speak so confidently about the sanctity of life until I imagined someone I loved enduring that horror. All I would think about was killing the man who did it. And suddenly, my moral certainty seemed so much easier to defend when the suffering belonged to someone else.

And every time I tried to settle comfortably into one side, I found myself calculating answers I could barely stand to say aloud. So that's why I don't go by the terms pro-choice or pro-life. I believe both early stages of human life and the dignity of the woman carrying it deserve reverence. Every circumstance between them deserves delicacy, humility, and compassion. We live in a state of imperfection. Be kind. All we have is each other.

text:
💿 My Top 90 Albums of the 90s #Top90AlbumsOfThe90s 

#50 #AlanisMorissette @Alanis – Jagged Little Pill

📅 Released: June 13, 1995

📊 Chart Peaks: 🇺🇸 #1 · 🇬🇧 #1 · 🇩🇪 #3

🏆 Biggest Single: “Ironic” – 🇺🇸 #4 · 🇬🇧 #11 · 🇩🇪 #8

🔝 Favorite Track: “Hand in My Pocket”

👨‍💻 My Take: Here’s to the Top 50! I know, I’m a day late, but I’ve had a lot going on – so let’s finally kick off the nifty fifty! 😁

And we begin with another remarkable female breakthrough – this time from the rock section. I had some second thoughts about the balance of this countdown and decided to bring in a few more rock albums here rather than later.

Strictly speaking, Jagged Little Pill wasn’t Alanis Morissette’s debut: she had already released two Canadian dance-pop albums. (Tell more about, @bsmntdwllr73 😁).  But it was her international breakthrough, her complete reinvention as a rock artist – and the album that introduced this Alanis to the world.

Today, #50 feels about right. As @GenTXer2  pointed out earlier, I do think Alanis has not aged so well after all – meaning Alanis, the angry young rock star hasn’t aged perfectly for me. This album was a force of nature and laid important groundwork for the wave of outspoken female singer-songwriters who followed. It was powerful, fearless and often brilliant – but occasionally also exhausting.

I have six clear favorites: “Hand in My Pocket” at the top, followed by “Perfect,” “You Learn,” “Mary Jane,” “Head Over Feet” and, of course, “Ironic” – although I have probably heard that one a few thousand times too often.

The rest is sometimes simply too much for me. Too much anger? Too much abrasive guitar rock? Not enough melody? I’m not entirely sure. But I often skip “You Oughta Know” – yes, I know that’s sacrilege! – as well as “Forgiven,” “Not the Doctor” and “Wake Up.”

Nothing is ever perfect – and that also applies to Alanis’ subsequent career. After this incredibly promising beginning, I continued buying every new album. There was no streaming or iTunes yet, after all: you bought the CD and hoped for the best. Usually, I found two or three strong songs but was disappointed by the albums as a whole.

Her catalogue certainly isn’t thin – you can easily assemble 15 to 20 very good Alanis songs. But for me, she never became better than she was here. At least she continued making music after her monumental breakthrough – unlike Lauryn Hill. 😉

That became especially clear to me in Vienna in 2012. Within two nights, I saw Bruce Springsteen at the Ernst Happel Stadium and Alanis at the Arena before we started our vacation to France. The comparison was brutal: the 62-year-old Boss delivered an electrifying marathon, while the 38-year-old Alanis seemed strangely flat and had surprisingly little to offer beyond the Jagged Little Pill classics.

Perhaps it was simply an off night. And who knows – maybe there is still another great Alanis chapter waiting somewhere. 😉

💭 Thoughts: Has Jagged Little Pill aged well for you – and did Alanis ever make another album that came close?

I spent my last crypto I had leftover since 2022  on groceries today ☺️

The only net worth i have is 5090, 4090, 3080, Vega 56, couple ryzen 9950x3d, 96 + 64 gb ddr5 ram, some ddr4, around 10tb ssd, 4 monitors, two electric guitars maybe $1000-1500 max for both.

That’s pretty much it.
Well, I do have flat in Volgograd, 3 room but it costs max $30k, half of it isn’t mine, and moving money to Poland via crypto is terribly hard.

So I never bought any stock since 2013 when I got first job 🫠
Money just keep disappearing due to different reasons.

So I guess the answer for me is to build something that will make more money I can earn on employment.

My first salary was $700/mo
Then $1500/mo
Around 2015 i started fully remote on oDesk it was $4/h
Then same year $8/h, then $12/h, then uncle Sean from Iowa found me and offered $500 a week, good times 2015-2016.
Then I got into UK product company 2500 gbp!
That was most peaceful time i ever had in dev… no deadlines no bullshit just sane consistent development, thoroughly slowly iterating on features and fixing bugs, they didn’t even had tests can you imagine?

Then I got into Ruby in 2018, back to $2000/mo.
Then 2021 it was $4000 suddenly, then end of year i was hired for $6000. It lasted couple months and then war started…

And so my highest salary was i think 8000 eur per month

Basically nothing, today’s money.
I don’t own a car, i dont go outside even, i stopped buying video games, the only thing is I upgraded PC that’s it largest thing I spent money on but also the only thing I use 100% of my conscious time.

I am literally broke 😤
But somehow still surviving 
In this economy!

Today I thought whether I should eat more meat or should I add more milk products. Around 800-1000 kcal daily is all I can afford.

And worst of it all is I bled all my savings to expensive apartment i dont have money to move out from lol 🤣

And what is really funny is that I can easily take a second job and recoup everything I lost in 6 months in just 4 months 🤷‍♂️

It works but super stressful i don’t recommend doing it. Working 16 hours a day isn’t sustainable.

Right now I am doing fine, getting used to read and delete code again😌

but man the bureaucracy of getting my invoice paid kills me 🫠
I thought November I don’t have to ask more money from my family — nope lol, enjoy slow burn🔥🔥🔥

I just wanna buy a new teapot ☺️
God, if you exist, can you make them approve my invoice 🙏

I mean, I need to pay VAT strict until November 25th or am gonna get into trouble, and it’s literally 23%

I was thinking of selling 5090 for months now, this might be it 🤣
It costs $10000 new one in Poland, i still have warranty lol
I bought it for like $2300 just a year ago… 

Anyway!
Thanks for reading my rants about capitalism.
It seems to work as intended, doesn’t need to be fixed.
It simply has to be dismantled ☺️

text:
Three House committee chairs just called Jensen Huang in for a closed-door briefing on November 18. Foreign Affairs, the China Select Committee, and Intelligence. All three at once.

Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford sent the letter on November 4. They want two things. Explain his interactions with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive U.S. intelligence assessed as a Chinese intelligence asset. And explain how Nvidia protects its technology from foreign espionage. He had until November 11 to accept or offer another date. It was a request, not a subpoena. By the 11th, lawmakers were already talking about issuing one if he didn’t show up himself.

The background is the New York Times report from October 29. Intelligence officials concluded Alice Huang was working for China’s Ministry of State Security while building a close relationship with Jensen. They are not related. Megaspeed’s Malaysian affiliate bought at least 4.8 billion dollars in Nvidia AI equipment between June 2024 and February 2026. Commerce Department investigators have been looking into whether any of it reached China. Jensen told employees on November 8 that he had been unfaithful to his wife. The board launched an independent investigation the same day and said it has no reason to believe company secrets were compromised.

On November 9, congressional leaders got a classified briefing that mostly focused on Iran. Nvidia came up briefly. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said there are real concerns that need a full separate briefing, and he supports tighter controls on advanced chips going to China in the annual defense bill.

Trump was first briefed on this roughly a year earlier, in late 2025. Marco Rubio oversaw a classified memo in the spring. In May, on Air Force One, Rubio warned him again before Huang joined the China trip. Trump later said the information didn’t make much of an impact. The question isn’t whether Congress is treating this as a national security issue. It is. The question is what the company and the administration knew, when they knew it, and what they did next. November 18 will tell us whether Jensen answers those questions himself.

text:
While we see a balanced speaker list for TPUSA’s upcoming AmericaFest, this belies a deep fracture within the organization. A lot has changed since Erika Kirk endorsed Vance for president at last year’s TPUSA AmFest. That early endorsement now forces the organization to try to coalesce around an increasingly controversial figure amid clear tensions on the right. 

Since that time, Vance has:

* Refused to distance himself from Tucker Carlson even as Carlson became increasingly radicalized and publicly floated whether Trump “could be the Antichrist” 

* Led and pushed hardest for ceasefires with Iran, taking America's foot off the gas just when Iran was at its weakest, thereby losing critical weeks and months, and effecting gas prices and eventually the midterms. 

* Drafted the disastrous MOU which lifted American pressure before the Islamic Republic delivered any irreversible concessions. The united States began removing its naval blockade, authorized Iranian oil sales and offered access to frozen assets. 

* Undermined political support for the war through public statements and association with the New Right, signaling to Iran that resistance could simply outlast U.S. resolve.

* Hired Mark Mitchell (a legit Groyper who accused Israel of assassinating Charlie Kirk) as the source of his polling data for his hit piece,  blaming the GOP loss on Israel. 

* Granted repeated access and interviews to figures associated with the New Right —including multiple sit-downs with Megyn Kelly and an exclusive Air Force Two interview with Jack Posobiec in October 2026, while maintaining a close personal loyalty to Tucker Carlson (refusing to “throw friends under the bus” even after Carlson’s attacks on Trump and Israel, and employing Carlson’s son in his orbit). 

* Publicly praised other New Right-adjacent voices such as Theo Von. At the same time, he has largely avoided or publicly rebuked traditional pro-Israel conservatives like Ben Shapiro (his closing speech at AmFest 2025 was widely read as a direct rejection of Shapiro’s call to name and distance from “frauds and grifters” such as Carlson and Owens), Mark Levin, and Marc Thiessen.

🚨 THWART CRIME #046 — STOW, OHIO

FOUR ARMED ROBBERS. ONE ARMED CLERK.

November 2, 2026

Four masked suspects arrived at a Circle K in stolen minivans around 3:30 AM, repeatedly ramming the storefront in an attempt to steal the ATM. They weren’t expecting 41-year-old overnight clerk Kendrick Watson.

Seeing the suspects approaching, Watson fired seven shots to protect himself and his coworker. The suspects fled.

One suspect was subsequently arrested, while the others remain under investigation. Watson faced no criminal charges.

BUT HERE’S THE TWIST…

Watson says the incident cost him his job after his employer initially took him off the schedule over the company’s weapons policy. text:
He mewed and purred about a few of the women on the secluded beaches, sampling some as he went, until he came across three dark haired thesapiens paddling in the shallows of the water. They were quite naked and clearly enjoying each other’s company as they were kissing and licking one another’s breasts. Chester perched himself in a nearby palm tree and peered at them through a telescope that rapidly grew in his hand.

The three ladies were so relaxed in each other’s presence that the licking soon gravitated south. The telescope grew again, and some humidity steamed up the lens. Chester quickly scampered down from the tree, removed his clothes, and joined the ladies in the still waters.

They were not pleased to see him.

At first, the ladies were resistant to his offer to clean them, and then resistant to his suggestion that he show them how to lick like a cat. In fact, it shocked Chester to learn that they had no interest in him at all, and that they were only interested in each other, and not in men. 

After some thought Chester realised that the women were confused and offered a free night in his company which would, according to Chester, undoubtedly cure them. The comment earned him quite a slap from the tallest of the brunettes. He could not understand it. This was new territory, and since it was new territory, Chester decided that perhaps it required marking. 

Chester was feeling quite full, having consumed a lot of blood from the more generous ladies of Seti and released a spray. The spray was prolific and not especially pleasant since he always ate onions with his tributes.

The ladies were a tad put out by it and all three set about him with their fists. The cat rushed to shore, quickly dressed and climbed back into his tree. The women ignored him as they sunk under the water desperately attempting to remove the stench of ammonia from their flesh. 

Chester removed his gloves briefly to lick his paws, then took a vial of clear fluid from the inner pocket of his jacket. 

He collected suspended infectious disease and bacteria. It was a hobby. His plush chambers behind the hall of mirrors in Corax consisted of a bed covered in black silk sheets and black shelves filled with such vials, each carefully marked. Chester always carried one or two vials on his person, alongside a bottle of sulphuric acid, just in case someone annoyed him.

As the ladies continued to cleanse themselves, Chester climbed down from the tree, unsealed the bottle and poured the clear fluid into the water. The label read ‘Accelerated Necrotising Fasciitis.’ He edged away from the water and sat on the sand watching.

At first there was scratching, then clawing, followed by gouges.

Chester was a natural and caring biocentric. He believed that certain bacteria had been oppressed by systemic exclusion, and the poor creatures deserved a place to thrive. Whilst laying on the beach looking at the suns, he had decided that necrotising fasciitis was disadvantaged by the most latent social exclusion and judgement, and that by pouring the dear little bacteria into the oasis he had created balance in this hideous disequilibrium.

It did not take long for additional bruises to appear and open as the gouges spread and lurked about the tormented bodies. It took less time for the flesh to strip back from the bone and the ladies to crawl onto the beach begging Chester to help them. Chester shook his head, smirked and held up the empty vial. By the time the ladies had realised what was happening, the disenfranchised bacteria had found, not only a new home, but a source of food. Chester was pleased for them.

As the ladies writhed and peeled on the beach, he created and sang The National Anthem for the Integration of Vulnerable Bacteria,
‘Oh, I can just see,
Your new home so be free.
Grow and feed preciously,
And spread abundantly.

Oh, chew your way through,
Wicked flesh as you do,
Leave the bones for the coup,
Good times are coming for you.

Bacteria be free,
And spread abundantly.’

As Chester sang his eloquent tune for the fourth time, the bacteria rejoiced in peeling the flesh from the faces of their victims. The still living bodies, flayed, gouged and chewed, glared at Chester through horrified eyes, widened by the absence of flesh. 

The sand was quite elated as the red tint from the blood made a change from the curse of constantly yellow grains.

Chester gave the ladies a cheerful wave, as they heaved and writhed about in their own minced flesh, and decided to return to Mira.

Mira, meanwhile, had taken Chester’s threesome idea under advisement, and on Chester’s return he found her being pounded from both ends by two lads on spring vacation. Chester was not amused. He had had a dreadful day, and the one soul he tried to save had betrayed him. You see, when Chester suggested the threesome, he assumed he would be included. The exclusion added further insult to all the other injuries Neferaten had inflicted upon him, causing great sorrow.

He watched from the sand dunes and waited until all was done. The lads took a quick dip in the oasis where many of Chester’s bacterium were waiting to make friends with them. He then approached Mira and led her lovingly to a rock pool. He lowered her in, scrubbed her as she had done to him. Licked her. Caressed her. Then climbed out and invigorated the water with sulphuric acid. He held Mira’s shoulders firmly and watched as she struggled and fizzed like one of Nicolas’s anti-cabbage effervescent tablets, until her insides were on the outside and she would betray him no more. 

A break-off beaver brigade continued to follow the sound of Chester’s flute as he headed for Khafre. 

The beavers caused an undue amount of mess on the way by chewing wood, digging holes and creating damns at rapid, vampiric speed. Their constant stopping delayed Chester’s flights and treks and caused him a little duress. He also blamed their presence for his heartbreak in Seti, as the ladies seemed more interested in beaver than in Chester’s magnificent flute. He decided that the errant break-off beaver horde needed a home, but so big was the horde that one home alone would not be suitable. 

Khafre sat on the border of Ard Quahila and Neferaten and was home to the source of The Elin. Chester encouraged some of the beavers to remain in Khafre and build new lives and vocations. The beaver were happy to do so, and with a load off of his shoulders, Chester was free to explore other interests.

His interests took the form of an obsession with the local armadillo sanctuary. Chester loved armadillos, especially the way their long fluffy noses sucked up ants. He also wanted to love the curvy veterinarian, Portia, who ran the sanctuary. After some engaging chat-up lines, and compliments about the size of her armadillos, Portia gave Chester a guided tour. She did explain on three occasions that the correct term for the armadillos was aardvarks, but Chester told her that taxonomy was his speciality and she had her ‘nomenclature confused.’ Given Chester’s suave confidence, and large hat, she decided to let it slide.

As they walked about the park, Portia explained the purposes of the aardvark’s long nose, and Chester responded by showing her something longer. Portia was so impressed that the two sampled each other’s company in the woods beyond the watering hole. Chester found her armadillos to be most agreeable, so much so that he returned a short while later. 

The sanctuary was closed, but this did not deter Chester. He located Portia in the local tavern offering her armadillos to other men for money. Chester was relieved that he had not had to part with any money but still found her morality somewhat lacking. 

An hour later the mayor of Khafre found the fence bordering Ard Quahila was damaged. A large section of the barbed wire had been removed, and Portia’s body was found wrapped in the same wire sporting a sign which said, ‘Crunchy Like a Dillo!’ 

Chester had managed to forget to close the sanctuary gate, and his flute attracted the aardvarks that he insisted on calling armadillos, and they followed his melody alongside the remaining beavers. Chester offered the armadillos a taste of his blood to prevent weariness.

The aardvarks, or armadillos, however you want to see them, caused a bigger disruption than the beavers on the next leg of Chester’s adventure. This leg took in the sights of Thutmose. 

On arrival in Thutmose, the monstrous aardvarks took to digging. They dug around the village, they dug around the irrigation systems, they dug up crops, and they dug under people’s houses. 

When approached by the local sheriff, Chester feigned ignorance about the origins of the influx of the armadillos. 

The sheriff, Sheriff Leanna of Thutmose, recently transferred from Sapari, called on the urgent expertise of one Detective Cedric. Detective Cedric had already had a very busy day dealing with a bizarre game of blade roulette in Serphage, and a troublesome woman in Sapari who was pestering beggars. 

Nicolai-Cedric arrived in his black cloak, holding a revoltingly large magnifying glass. He inspected the armadillos thoroughly, whilst nodding. He concluded that the armadillos were in need of food and were clearly blood drinkers. Chester concurred even though no one asked. 

Leanna informed both Cedric and Chester that the creatures were aardvarks not armadillos.

Cedric took great offense at this sort of talk and reminded Leanna that her negativity towards the great people of the armadillo community offended both the vigilante milkmaids and the ink-eaters of Neferaten. He proposed further that such offences attracted a fine of one meal for three, and he did not mean the eating sort. Leanna told him not to be so disgusting, and sent both him and Chester, who was equally enthusiastic about the fine, packing. 

Later that day, Detective Cedric was called back to the sheriff station to investigate the untimely death of the sheriff, who appeared to suffer multiple stab wounds that the coroner attributed to three male serial killers from Threnodyl. Cedric proposed replacing the sheriff with the sheriff of Shaenaten, which was done, and shortly after the coroner’s daughter disappeared, and Cedric and Chester got their menage a trois.

Once the great detective Cedric had wrapped up the bizarre mysteries of Neferaten, including the death of Portia, which he determined was self-inflicted for sexual gratification, Chester was free to leave Neferaten.

Chester returned to Corax exhausted by the whole mess, only to find some nutter prowling about his hall of mirrors. Nicolas had left him a glorious gift. He took the nutter to his chambers and turned her into what he called a Poke Bowl.

That same evening Lilith received a complaint from Tiye regarding rabid beavers and a glassblower who had sucked instead of blown. Lilith forwarded the matter to Tepes, as she considered Theaten too stupid to handle such matters. 

Tepes received a second letter from the lords of Shepsut about an outbreak of tapeworm, that he replied was not his problem as he managed the Kingdom of Tepes not Neferaten and proposed contacting the veterinarian, Portia. 

Unfortunately, Portia could not be bothered to reply. 

Tepes then received another letter from Lilith complaining about skin diseases, aardvarks digging holes and the tardiness of her laundry. Tepes, who was sick of being the national complaints committee sent all communications via raven to Theaten. 

Theaten could not answer as he had spent the entire afternoon in the bank trying to explain why his identity card said Theaten and not Robert. 

Klouthe took the initiative to forward the letters to Nicolas. Nicolai-Binky read them and gave them to Chives with instructions to have the porters dump them in the drains of Ashurrel alongside the bones of some slightly insane, but silent, bank managers, and a few broken clocks that Nicolas had left laying around.

Act II: The Jester and The Immoless

Scene I; Prelude, The Pied Piper and The Beavers

The 2nd Day of the 4th Moon, 1536 P.V.
Sapari

During the small hours, a messenger arrived in Sapari on horseback. The horse was somewhat foolish looking. It appeared to grin and had huge goofy teeth. The new harbour master, a young man named Billy Botwell who had been dispatched from Threnodyl after the strange disappearance of the old harbour master, tried not to stare. He considered staring rude but could not help glancing every now and then at the strange beast. He even smiled at the horse in a moment of awkwardness, and the horse grinned back, making him feel even more awkward. 

The situation worsened when a raven swooped down, landed on the quayside next to the horse, spilled in a heap of guts and bones and a red-headed pied piper, Chester, stepped out from the debris. 

Chester grew to his full height as the raven reassembled itself. Billy rubbed his eyes in disbelief, put the whole experience down to the Ashurrel leaf he was chewing, and spat it on the walkway.

‘That’s government property you’re soiling there!’ Chester pointed out with some force, squaring up to the poor little lad. The messenger riding the overfriendly horse, who was clad in purple and wore an eye patch, waved a hand at Chester,
‘Easy now, the lad is clearly new!’ 

The messenger smiled at the lad, the lad smiled back, and the messenger’s smile dropped,
‘Pick it up! Ya filthy landlubber!’ 
Billy dropped to his knees and scooped up the damp leaves, and not knowing what to do with them shoved them back into his mouth and gagged.

The messenger ignored the retching and got straight down to business. He informed the new harbour master that his name was Bigglesworth, Commodore Bigglesworth or Commodore Nicolas Bigglesworth, and stated that he had ridden through the night along the coast to relay an urgent message. Pirates were headed to Sapari. Not a single pirate ship, but several, a fleet in fact. An armada. The pirates, Nicolai-Bigglesworth claimed, were intending to steal wood from the shipyard. 

Billy did not think to ask where the message had emanated from or who had ordered its forwarding as he was still uneasy about the whole grinning horse and raven splatter debacle. 

Once the message had been relayed, and Bigglesworth’s first job of the day accomplished, Bigglesworth turned to Chester and explained his next job of the day,
‘The Immoless!’ He stated, without further explanation.
‘Neferaten,’ Chester replied. 

Chester then crouched down and the bone, guts and feathers of the same raven that had disturbed Billy, split apart, engulfed Chester and flew away at a speed only animals dosed with vampire blood could manage. Billy watched with his mouth agape, annoying Bigglesworth,
‘Well, boy! Don’t just stand staring, get the message out.’ 
Billy nodded and acted immediately. 

Bigglesworth made haste on Nicolas’s goofy vampiric horse, Zimba, along the quayside, bypassed the town and rode into the Dokeshi Carnival where he tethered the horse. He then summoned the guardians of Dokeshi, two demonic clown lovers, Scurra and Phylax to stand guard. Once the demons were in position, Bigglesworth crouched and allowed an albatross to absorb him and flew out to The Sombre.

The harbour master, who was a little disturbed by all the carry on, immediately sent word to the shipyard, and advised that they move the wood, via a caravan, to the village of Ashurrel that bordered Togaduine. This, Billy reasoned, was the only logical course of action as Ashurrel was far from port. He did not want the workers to enter Togaduine as, it was believed, a tyrant ruled the kingdom. A tyrant based in Corax Asylum. The labourers at the shipyard acted immediately.

Nonetheless, the new harbour master, being a bit of a jobsworth, decided to undertake every precaution. He declared that all ships should leave port and anchor together building an impenetrable wall on the horizon, whilst avoiding the local fishermen to prevent produce diminishment. It just so happened that the same harbour master had been gifted a cargo of anchors not a week before, from the brand ‘Ferromagnetic DeSilva,’ at least that is what the boxes said.

The ships formed their wall, and used the anchors to secure their positions, but it became apparent by late afternoon that there was no pirate armada, and the ships attempted to return to shore. However, somewhere there was a reversal of polarity in the magnetic anchors and the ships slammed together crunching the hulls, buckling the decks, and causing a huge mess in the ocean. The debris was formidable, and everyone forgot about the wood. 

When Billy finally dispatched a caravan to retrieve the wood they found it quite gone. Everyone was disgruntled, but before any investigation got underway Billy met an untimely death after a three ton anchor fell on his oversized head from a crane winch. The new harbour master soon became the old harbour master, and a harbour master from Ashurrel was sent to replace him, which was a little odd as Ashurrel had no proximity to the ocean. It was also a little odd that the new harbour master sported green locks, had eight eyes and called himself, ‘Rachnoc.’ The dock workers did not know what to make of Nicolai-Rachnoc and his excess of eyes, and rumours soon flew about that he was a loony recently escaped from Corax Asylum. The rumours were started by a dock labourer named Samson. The rumours stopped when Samson’s intestines accidentally released themselves from his body and wrapped around the drum of a dodgy capstan.

The Lord of Sapari wrote to Tepes to complain about the entire matter, and Tepes wrote to Theaten. Theaten forwarded his concerns to Nicolas by raven, and said letter was dumped, along with a few body parts, into the drains at Ashurrel. 

No one knew who was responsible for the Ferromagnetic anchors, but some recognised the horse. And there were rumours.

There were also rumours about Chester. Some claimed that the love god, who’s reputation preceded him, was a legend. Others believed he was Nicolas, or a cad, or a monster, and others still considered him to be an opportunistic postman. All rumours were, in fact, partially correct.

Chester was an infamous demon, infamous in Irkalla, and infamous in Corax Asylum, who Nicolas called the ‘The Pied Piper’ on account of the amount of beaver that followed him desperately trying to blow his massive flute. Nicolas was often jealous of Chester’s success with the ladies and put it down to his unusual appearance and impeccable taste. Chester was, in fact, a special Nicolai. He was the embodiment of Nicolas’s libido, his Evro, a walking dick and balls with the gift of the gab, and the skillset to match. 

During the snowy first moon of 1536 P.V., Chester had spent his time building up a following of sorts around Neferaten. He moved from village to village keeping the ladies of every occupation and class warm. He found that dressing as a postman opened doors, and legs, with very little explanation needed. His raven allowed him to move swiftly between villages and broaden his portfolio of conquests. He had intended to return to his ladies sooner, but Nicolas insisted that he spent the second and third moon with Allyra on account of Nicolas and the prolific scientist and strategist Nicolai-Webster developing the new plan, Plan BAT, Belua Alvearis Tyrannus.

This restriction on Chester’s movements caused a day of yowling, sulking and whining, but Nicolas flipped his two-headed coin for the job, and Chester lost. Chester considered Nicolas and Webster’s plans to be a waste of time as previous plans and procedures to alleviate the recurring problem troubling the Nicolai had failed. 

Webster called the problem Alveus Vacuus Problemus or AVP for short. 

Several plans had been executed over several centuries, and all failed with quite horrific consequences. Nicolas and Webster had really upped the ante during the previous five years, but their plans continued to backfire. Webster blamed Nicolas, and Nicolas blamed Webster. Chester did not care who blamed who, he cared that his balls were temporarily in a sling. Nonetheless, he did adhere to the new plan and spent two moons being the perfect boyfriend. Of course, he had been Allyra’s ‘perfect’ boyfriend for the past five years, but he diligently increased love-bombing and worrying Allyra with his fake sympathy, mesmerism and coercion to enhance that appearance for Nicolas’s sake. 

You see, Dear Reader, part of the problem worrying the Nicolai was that they did not have a queen, and part of the solution, Nicolas decided, involved taking a bride, and he had idealistic notions of how this should play out. These notions stemmed largely from his prolific reading of Carmilla Fanu’s dark romance novels. Nicolas somehow convinced himself that he was the dark handsome prince, protecting women from his own wrath. You could say that he misinterpreted the ideas behind the novels as he was conflicted in the realistic conveyance of the tropes. 

Nicolas understood that first he had to be the beast, and threatening, and then he had to also be the dark, morally grey, romantic hero redeemed by love. Unfortunately, Nicolas failed to realise that these novels were fiction, and that the heroes were not nearly as repulsive as he was. The repulsive beast came quite naturally to Nicolas, but the hero side not so much, and he had no interest in personal redemption of any sort. He also failed to correctly comprehend the order of the narrative functions. In practise this meant that most of the time his would-be brides were dead by Nicolas the Monster’s hand before Nicolas the Prince rocked up to save them.

Nicolas also misunderstood the word ‘no’ and interpreted it as the ‘princess’ being coy or shy, so when the potential bride reacted to his advances with some hostility, the beast became extraordinarily perturbed, and as such most of his plans failed spectacularly.

Now, Dear Reader, I have digressed a little from the prelude, or prologue, you may view it either way. This prelude focuses on the sufferings of Chester not the stupid ideas of Nicolas, so let us return to that. 

Nicolas was more than ready to descend upon Allyra, show her the beast and the prince, and generally make her life difficult until she fell in love with him. Since Nicolas had planned a busy day of annoying Allyra, or as Nicolas called it, ‘seducing the Immoless’ Chester was free to revisit the pussies of the ladies of Neferaten and secretly get Allyra back for hitting Nicolas with a metal rod.

Unfortunately for poor Chester, the ladies had moved on. 

Chester was quite happy to cheat and roam locating new conquests, and equally happy to dump any woman on a whim, but he did not take well to being the recipient of the same treatment.

He blamed the loose virtues of the women, not the manipulative natures of the men, for these atrocities and reacted with the wrath of a creature forlorn and broken-hearted by such cruel rejections.

The 2nd Day of the 4th Moon, 1536 P.V.
Neferaten

Chester took a detour to Corax, after his stopgap at Sapari, to change into his postman’s uniform, then flew directly to Tiye where hordes of beaver awaited his return. 

The beavers had arrived in Neferaten during the first moon of the year. They had followed Chester there, as beaver followed Chester everywhere, it was a burden he had to bear. The beaver remained in Tiye where they dropped logs and dug holes.

Chester had not gone to Tiye to meet the beavers. Nonetheless, he did lead them quickly to a watering hole by one of the bridges and blessed them by biting his own wrist and adding a few drops of blood to the water for the sake of their virility and fertility. That was what he claimed anyway.

Chester actually returned to Tiye to meet with the beautiful thesapien glassblower, Thalia. Thalia had fascinatingly bobbed, brown hair with thick streaks of ginger, which Chester approved of, and was able to examine in some detail as he spent most of his time with Thalia during the first moon, staring at the top of her head or watching himself fuck her in the glass. He liked the ginger in her hair as he liked women who reminded him of himself. Chester had spent the entire first week of the first moon with Thalia who demonstrated her prolific blowing skills on him. She also showed him the processes surrounding glass manufacturing. 

Although Nicolas had only offered Chester a day to hump his way through Neferaten on this occasion, a challenge Chester was more than capable of meeting, he had hoped to see Thalia’s head one last time before ending their courtship. 

Chester desperately wanted to surprise Thalia with his magnificent presence, and even considered railing her with his gloriously long tongue as a thank you. As such, our cat walked the circumference of the warehouse, climbed up the outer wall to the window and peered in. 

Chester liked to spy and stare, it was a common trait among the Immortalis who framed it as reasonably protective and caring behaviour as opposed to downright creepy and wrong. 

Thalia was busy blowing pipes, but there was no glass involved. Instead, she was blowing the pipes of the tanner and the cheesemaker, at the same time. It was one thing for Chester to romance three or four women at once, but for a woman to do it with multiple men seemed crude and outrageous. This, however, did not stop Chester staring, and one hand took a wander into his pants as the other paw clawed into the woodwork keeping him balanced. 

Passers-by opted not to look up as rumour had it that the sadist Nicolas masqueraded as a postman or a pied piper, also the people of The Deep were also used to postmen slipping more than letters into the women’s boxes.

Once all loads had been blown, Chester decided to pay Thalia a visit to confront her about her infidelity, even though they were not in a relationship. He waited until both men made their hasty departure, purchased a large jug of iced water to cool his temper from a street seller who wore a yellow and black robe and called himself Robert, then addressed his concerns with Thalia before her employees arrived. 

Thalia was unrepentant and annoyed, as if it was Chester’s fault that she was a hoe. During her angry rant, in which she attributed a comprehensive compendium of unpleasant nouns to Chester, Thalia inhaled so sharply and viciously that somehow molten glass just leapt from its crucible and into her mouth. The force of entry was so great that it spewed down her throat, followed closely by a glass jar of iced water. 

Chester rammed the glass in so hard that it cracked, tearing her lips, and mouth open. He pushed and rotated his hand continually until the whole container sat in shards in Thalia’s mouth and throat. The ice sizzled against the molten glass. Thalia’s eyes rolled back into white orbs as she tried to scream, but only steam came out. Then angry shards of glass desperately tried to escape their captivity by ripping through her throat. Her twitching body collapsed to the floor. More steam pumped out through the newly splayed orifices allowing Thalia to blow as much as she desired.

Chester was heartbroken. And hungry. His face elongated, his eyes narrowed and shone a ravenous emerald. As Thalia lay convulsing, Chester raised her skirt, pulled down her fine thong, and, after some exploration and tasting with his thick black tongue bit into her mound. She retched a few final attempts at breathing, then stilled. Chester took another bite, then another, swallowing the meat and blood as only a refined gentleman could. 

His thirst unexpectedly experienced additional satisfaction through the consumption of the thick blood provided by the moonly rationale for her offering only head to her suitors on that glorious day. This pleased Chester and he decided to have a quick goodbye fuck for luck. There was not much left to fuck, but he managed to locate the remains of two orifices that sat close together and this sufficed.

Chester bored of Tiye as soon as Thalia’s employees started showing up. The people were constant whingers. They complained about the loss of their chief glassblower, they complained about the beavers ‘upsetting the ecosystem,’ Chester didn’t even know what that meant, and they complained about the locusts that seemed to like Chester’s favourite aftershave. His aftershave was a bespoke and expensive number based on the erotic smell of rotting cabbages. The ladies seemed to like it too, or at least they met with an untimely demise if his taste in essences was brought into question. 

When Chester tired of the moaning, he changed course and travelled east to the village of Shepsut playing a merry tune from within his raven.

Some of the beavers remained in Tiye and some of the beavers followed.

The village of Shepsut operated both the grain stores and the laundry. Lilith did not care to do her own laundry, and despised the sight of washing lines, so all laundry in Shaenaten was sent to Shepsut. The Shepsutians made money, and Lilith did not have to look at the mess. This suited everyone. 

During his first moon in Neferaten, Chester had fallen in love with all the ladies of the grain store. On his return, and feeling irritably amorous, he discovered, after a little foreplay with three or four of his lovers, that a rather repulsive worm outbreak had occurred in places where worms ought not to be. 

Chester blamed the ink-eaters of the area who treated the granary as a brothel, and the brothel as another brothel, for the outbreak. The ink-eaters were renowned snobs, all of whom had families and worked in banking. 

The DeSilva Banks were operated by Pauley the Cheese and Nicolas’s public relations Nicolai, the black suited media mogul Monsieur Silas Gideon Alaric Bartholomew-Crispin (with a hyphen) Ledgerly. 

Ledgerly and Pauley had specifically noted on all contracts that employees were banned from having worms, lice, scabies or chlamydia. It seemed to Chester that the ink-eaters had failed to keep their end of the contract. He sent word via raven to Chives that the tertiary horde of Nicolai were to be dispatched to all branches and would take over immediately as managers given the obvious lapse in employee standards. 

Chives prepared the carriages. 

Ledgerly, who had just returned from Serphage with a printing job for Corax’s resident ghostwriter Nicolai-Bink ‘Binky’ McSnort regarding some inappropriate shenanigans by the coast, and Pauley the Cheese who had a day off from dosing the boars at the racetrack, went from town to town taking the third horde of Nicolai to the respective banks where they were immediately all declared manager. 

Pauley informed the staff of each branch, whilst he and Ledgerly had a little taste of the secretaries, that, in all branches, the new manger was called Mr Robert Robert. Nicolas had no issue in giving the Nicolai the same, or similar names. Several of the Nicolai were intentionally given variations of the name Nic, so that Nicolas could effectively praise himself when he praised them. 

The old bank managers were immediately declared insane and returned to Corax as a snack for the vampires. Each Robert Robert then directed the staff of each branch to change Theaten’s name on all paperwork to Lord Robert Robert of Robert. 

Chester could not let the matter of the worms rest. He was so hurt that the ladies he loved had tried to infect him that he introduced his favourite couple, Terry and Teresa Tapeworm to the grain stores.

In a moment of compassion, however, Chester decided to take his favourite laundry operator, the scrubber Mira, from Shepsut to the beautiful oasis of Seti, in the north, to save her virtue from the old and new worm outbreaks. He even allowed her to fly with him by raven. 

Some of the beavers followed with a haste only seen in creatures gifted with Immortalis or vampire blood.

Once at the oasis, Mira scrubbed Chester all over, polished and fiddled his flute, and swallowed every last note. Chester had trained her well and decided to train her further with a delicious threesome. On informing Mira of this idea, she seemed a little less enthusiastic about Chester, but he was determined to pursue the matter and scuttled off to find some nice women open to joining in.

text:
Immortalis Book One: The Jester and The Immoless
Act One

Scene XIII: Postlude, The Interruption

Corax Asylum, Togaduine
The 1st Day of the 4th Moon, 1536 P.V.

Nicolas was fuming. He had been quite happy holding Allyra and tricking her into subconsciously believing all sorts of revelations as she slept, whilst sneaking the odd fondle, when Ghorab arrived with an urgent letter. The letter read,

‘Sir,

Apologies. You must return to Corax immediately. Urgent. Apologies. Sorry.

Ever Loyal,
Chives.’

Nicolas knew that Chives would not dare disturb him unless the matter was of the utmost importance. He did not want to leave Allyra alone on The Sombre due to the sausage fest in the Clachdhu Beacon. He therefore quickly scribbled a note to Bigglesworth, who had already received his first job of the impending new day which involved a visit to Sapari. Nicolas’s letter read,

‘Commodore,

Once the pirate alarm is raised, check on our bride. She is aboard The Sombre.

N.’

Ghorab took the letter and made haste with it, and Nicolas travelled by his transport raven, Ghorab the Second, an innovative and long-considered name, directly to Corax. He spent the speedy journey lamenting leaving Allyra and winding himself up over the annoyance of the interruption. By the time he arrived and ‘de-feathered,’ as he called it, Nicolas was in a royal stonk of a mood.

Chives was waiting at the door of the main entrance,
‘Sir, I am so sorry, but he would not wait. He says he must speak with you right this second.’
Nicolas fiddled with the hole in his pants,
‘I want my new suit fetched forthwith.’
‘Very good, Sir. I have left him in your office.’
‘Who exactly have you left alone in my private office, Chives?’
‘Your son, Sir.’
Nicolas rolled his eyes and sighed,
‘What does he want?’
Chives fidgeted awkwardly,
‘I will have your suit collected immediately, Sir.’
‘Fine,’ Nicolas snapped, ‘I will find out myself.’

Nicolas threw open the office door to find Behmor sitting on HIS chair.
‘Son, move!’ Nicolas said.
Behmor stood and walked around the other side of the desk and sat down in the smaller chair, which strained and moaned under his weight.

Nicolas eyeballed Behmor as he marched, head held high, to his own chair, and threw himself down.

‘Something amiss father?’ Behmor asked.
‘Yes, something is amiss. I was busy attending to important errands, and I got summoned like a dog back here because you got the urge to invade my chair.’
‘No father, I needed a little chat regarding legal matters and current events.’
‘Current events don’t interest me, Behmor, I have told you this before. I prefer raisins.’
Behmor laid back in the chair and performed a half-smile,
‘Is there anything you want to tell me, father?’
‘If I wanted to tell you something, I would summon you, not the other way around.’
‘Then I shall get to the point, you cannot marry the third Immoless so end it now.’

Nicolas’s eyes glowed red, he lowered his gaze, then breathed out for far longer than necessary,
‘Chives told you, didn’t he?’
Behmor leaned forward,
‘It doesn’t matter who told me or how I found out, this must stop.’
‘No,’ Nicolas replied, ‘you wouldn’t care if it was your uncle, would you?’
‘Theaten is easier to manage and is built very differently to you.’
‘So, it is alright for Robert, but not for me?’
‘You are unpredictable, and unmanageable, and his name is Theaten.’
Nicolas swung on his chair,
‘His name is Robert.’
‘You see, this is what I mean. Unmanageable.’

Nicolas was not getting his own way and the sorrow filled expression arrived of its own accord,
‘You just want your poor fathers to be lonely! You don’t care that our hearts will break.’
Behmor raised an eyebrow,
‘Don’t bother, father.’
Nicolas immediately changed his expression from sadness to an evil smirk,
‘Sulphur rain is such a harsh thing. Terrible when it beats down in Irkalla. Worse if a rock hit Baal.’
‘And don’t threaten me!’
‘I don’t make threats. That was a promise.’
Behmor rubbed his chin,
‘Whatever you are up to, it stops now.’

Nicolas quickly changed the subject,
‘On another matter, find out who Lucien Nerison is.’

Behmor sighed heavily, and pulled a mirror from his jacket pocket,
‘Baal. Baal, I know you are listening!’
‘Yes,’ Baal replied.
‘Look up Lucien Nerison for me, find out anything that may be relevant to my father’s newest obsession, the third Immoless.’
‘Give me two minutes,’ Baal said, then smoke filled the glass.

Nicolas glared at Behmor. Behmor glared at Nicolas,
‘Father, end it. These poor women go through enough, a necessary evil, but I see no benefit in making her life even more miserable, do you? She has whatever you and your good selves plan on putting her through, and then Irkalla to look forward to.’
Nicolas sneered,
‘Don’t get sentimental on me, Behmor. I know what you get up to with your tributes, so don’t play innocent. Hot pokers. Stretching racks. Scarification. I wonder if Baal knows. How would your best friend and mentor feel if he knew your proclivities?’
Behmor rolled his eyes to the ceiling and shook his head,
‘Ridiculous.’

‘Sweetie,’ Baal muttered as the smoke cleared in the mirror, ‘Lucien Nerison asked for Allyra’s hand in marriage in 1532 and her father denied his request on the grounds of it conflicting with her position as Immoless.’
‘See father, nothing to worry about,’ Behmor said. He looked from the mirror to Nicolas who’s eyes were fully white. Drool and blood dripped from his mouth, and he growled in five furious voices continuously. The growl went on for two minutes, then Behmor interrupted,
‘I see you have taken the news that someone I have forbidden you from pursuing opted not to marry a different man four years ago with the maturity and sense I expected of you, father.’

Curtain Fall

text:
It’s not easy being one of Silicon Valley’s favorite benchmarks. 

SWE-Bench (pronounced “swee bench”) launched in November 2024 to evaluate an AI model’s coding skill, using more than 2,000 real-world programming problems pulled from the public GitHub repositories of 12 different Python-based projects. 

In the months since then, it’s quickly become one of the most popular tests in AI. A SWE-Bench score has become a mainstay of major model releases from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google—and outside of foundation models, the fine-tuners at AI firms are in constant competition to see who can rise above the pack. The top of the leaderboard is a pileup between three different fine tunings of Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet model and Amazon’s Q developer agent. Auto Code Rover—one of the Claude modifications—nabbed the number two spot in November, and was acquired just three months later.

Despite all the fervor, this isn’t exactly a truthful assessment of which model is “better.” As the benchmark has gained prominence, “you start to see that people really want that top spot,” says John Yang, a researcher on the team that developed SWE-Bench at Princeton University. As a result, entrants have begun to game the system—which is pushing many others to wonder whether there’s a better way to actually measure AI achievement.

Developers of these coding agents aren’t necessarily doing anything as straightforward cheating, but they’re crafting approaches that are too neatly tailored to the specifics of the benchmark. The initial SWE-Bench test set was limited to programs written in Python, which meant developers could gain an advantage by training their models exclusively on Python code. Soon, Yang noticed that high-scoring models would fail completely when tested on different programming languages—revealing an approach to the test that he describes as “gilded.”

“It looks nice and shiny at first glance, but then you try to run it on a different language and the whole thing just kind of falls apart,” Yang says. “At that point, you’re not designing a software engineering agent. You’re designing to make a SWE-Bench agent, which is much less interesting.”

The SWE-Bench issue is a symptom of a more sweeping—and complicated—problem in AI evaluation, and one that’s increasingly sparking heated debate: The benchmarks the industry uses to guide development are drifting further and further away from evaluating actual capabilities, calling their basic value into question. Making the situation worse, several benchmarks, most notably FrontierMath and Chatbot Arena, have recently come under heat for an alleged lack of transparency. Nevertheless, benchmarks still play a central role in model development, even if few experts are willing to take their results at face value. OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy recently described the situation as “an evaluation crisis”: the industry has fewer trusted methods for measuring capabilities and no clear path to better ones. 

“Historically, benchmarks were the way we evaluated AI systems,” says Vanessa Parli, director of research at Stanford University’s Institute for Human-Centered AI. “Is that the way we want to evaluate systems going forward? And if it’s not, what is the way?”

A growing group of academics and AI researchers are making the case that the answer is to go smaller, trading sweeping ambition for an approach inspired by the social sciences. Specifically, they want to focus more on testing validity, which for quantitative social scientists refers to how well a given questionnaire measures what it’s claiming to measure—and, more fundamentally, whether what it is measuring has a coherent definition. That could cause trouble for benchmarks assessing hazily defined concepts like “reasoning” or “scientific knowledge”—and for developers aiming to reach the much–hyped goal of artificial general intelligence—but it would put the industry on firmer ground as it looks to prove the worth of individual models.

“Taking validity seriously means asking folks in academia, industry, or wherever to show that their system does what they say it does,” says Abigail Jacobs, a University of Michigan professor who is a central figure in the new push for validity. “I think it points to a weakness in the AI world if they want to back off from showing that they can support their claim.”

The limits of traditional testing

If AI companies have been slow to respond to the growing failure of benchmarks, it’s partially because the test-scoring approach has been so effective for so long. 

One of the biggest early successes of contemporary AI was the ImageNet challenge, a kind of antecedent to contemporary benchmarks. Released in 2010 as an open challenge to researchers, the database held more than 3 million images for AI systems to categorize into 1,000 different classes.

Crucially, the test was completely agnostic to methods, and any successful algorithm quickly gained credibility regardless of how it worked. When an algorithm called AlexNet broke through in 2012, with a then unconventional form of GPU training, it became one of the foundational results of modern AI. Few would have guessed in advance that AlexNet’s convolutional neural nets would be the secret to unlocking image recognition—but after it scored well, no one dared dispute it. (One of AlexNet’s developers, Ilya Sutskever, would go on to cofound OpenAI.)

A large part of what made this challenge so effective was that there was little practical difference between ImageNet’s object classification challenge and the actual process of asking a computer to recognize an image. Even if there were disputes about methods, no one doubted that the highest-scoring model would have an advantage when deployed in an actual image recognition system.

But in the 12 years since, AI researchers have applied that same method-agnostic approach to increasingly general tasks. SWE-Bench is commonly used as a proxy for broader coding ability, while other exam-style benchmarks often stand in for reasoning ability. That broad scope makes it difficult to be rigorous about what a specific benchmark measures—which, in turn, makes it hard to use the findings responsibly. 

Where things break down

Anka Reuel, a PhD student who has been focusing on the benchmark problem as part of her research at Stanford, has become convinced the evaluation problem is the result of this push toward generality. “We’ve moved from task-specific models to general-purpose models,” Reuel says. “It’s not about a single task anymore but a whole bunch of tasks, so evaluation becomes harder.”

Like the University of Michigan’s Jacobs, Reuel thinks “the main issue with benchmarks is validity, even more than the practical implementation,” noting: “That’s where a lot of things break down.” For a task as complicated as coding, for instance, it’s nearly impossible to incorporate every possible scenario into your problem set. As a result, it’s hard to gauge whether a model is scoring better because it’s more skilled at coding or because it has more effectively manipulated the problem set. And with so much pressure on developers to achieve record scores, shortcuts are hard to resist.

For developers, the hope is that success on lots of specific benchmarks will add up to a generally capable model. But the techniques of agentic AI mean a single AI system can encompass a complex array of different models, making it hard to evaluate whether improvement on a specific task will lead to generalization. “There’s just many more knobs you can turn,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist at Princeton and a prominent critic of sloppy practices in the AI industry. “When it comes to agents, they have sort of given up on the best practices for evaluation.”

In a paper from last July, Kapoor called out specific issues in how AI models were approaching the WebArena benchmark, designed by Carnegie Mellon University researchers in 2024 as a test of an AI agent’s ability to traverse the web. The benchmark consists of more than 800 tasks to be performed on a set of cloned websites mimicking Reddit, Wikipedia, and others. Kapoor and his team identified an apparent hack in the winning model, called STeP. STeP included specific instructions about how Reddit structures URLs, allowing STeP models to jump directly to a given user’s profile page (a frequent element of WebArena tasks).

This shortcut wasn’t exactly cheating, but Kapoor sees it as “a serious misrepresentation of how well the agent would work had it seen the tasks in WebArena for the first time.” Because the technique was successful, though, a similar policy has since been adopted by OpenAI’s web agent Operator. (“Our evaluation setting is designed to assess how well an agent can solve tasks given some instruction about website structures and task execution,” an OpenAI representative said when reached for comment. “This approach is consistent with how others have used and reported results with WebArena.” STeP did not respond to a request for comment.)

Further highlighting the problem with AI benchmarks, late last month Kapoor and a team of researchers wrote a paper that revealed significant problems in Chatbot Arena, the popular crowdsourced evaluation system. According to the paper, the leaderboard was being manipulated; many top foundation models were conducting undisclosed private testing and releasing their scores selectively.

Today, even ImageNet itself, the mother of all benchmarks, has started to fall victim to validity problems. A 2023 study from researchers at the University of Washington and Google Research found that when ImageNet-winning algorithms were pitted against six real-world data sets, the architecture improvement “resulted in little to no progress,” suggesting that the external validity of the test had reached its limit.

Going smaller

For those who believe the main problem is validity, the best fix is reconnecting benchmarks to specific tasks. As Reuel puts it, AI developers “have to resort to these high-level benchmarks that are almost meaningless for downstream consumers, because the benchmark developers can’t anticipate the downstream task anymore.” So what if there was a way to help the downstream consumers identify this gap?

In November 2024, Reuel launched a public ranking project called BetterBench, which rates benchmarks on dozens of different criteria, such as whether the code has been publicly documented. But validity is a central theme, with particular criteria challenging designers to spell out what capability their benchmark is testing and how it relates to the tasks that make up the benchmark.

“You need to have a structural breakdown of the capabilities,” Reuel says. “What are the actual skills you care about, and how do you operationalize them into something we can measure?”

The results are surprising. One of the highest-scoring benchmarks is also the oldest: the Arcade Learning Environment (ALE), established in 2013 as a way to test models’ ability to learn how to play a library of Atari 2600 games. One of the lowest-scoring is the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) benchmark, a widely used test for general language skills; by the standards of BetterBench, the connection between the questions and the underlying skill was too poorly defined.

BetterBench hasn’t meant much for the reputations of specific benchmarks, at least not yet; MMLU is still widely used, and ALE is still marginal. But the project has succeeded in pushing validity into the broader conversation about how to fix benchmarks. In April, Reuel quietly joined a new research group hosted by Hugging Face, the University of Edinburgh, and EleutherAI, where she’ll develop her ideas on validity and AI model evaluation with other figures in the field. (An official announcement is expected later this month.) 

Irene Solaiman, Hugging Face’s head of global policy, says the group will focus on building valid benchmarks that go beyond measuring straightforward capabilities. “There’s just so much hunger for a good benchmark off the shelf that already works,” Solaiman says. “A lot of evaluations are trying to do too much.”

Increasingly, the rest of the industry seems to agree. In a paper in March, researchers from Google, Microsoft, Anthropic, and others laid out a new framework for improving evaluations—with validity as the first step. 

“AI evaluation science must,” the researchers argue, “move beyond coarse grained claims of ‘general intelligence’ towards more task-specific and real-world relevant measures of progress.” 

Measuring the “squishy” things

To help make this shift, some researchers are looking to the tools of social science. A February position paper argued that “evaluating GenAI systems is a social science measurement challenge,” specifically unpacking how the validity systems used in social measurements can be applied to AI benchmarking. 

The authors, largely employed by Microsoft’s research branch but joined by academics from Stanford and the University of Michigan, point to the standards that social scientists use to measure contested concepts like ideology, democracy, and media bias. Applied to AI benchmarks, those same procedures could offer a way to measure concepts like “reasoning” and “math proficiency” without slipping into hazy generalizations.

In the social science literature, it’s particularly important that metrics begin with a rigorous definition of the concept measured by the test. For instance, if the test is to measure how democratic a society is, it first needs to establish a definition for a “democratic society” and then establish questions that are relevant to that definition. 

To apply this to a benchmark like SWE-Bench, designers would need to set aside the classic machine learning approach, which is to collect programming problems from GitHub and create a scheme to validate answers as true or false. Instead, they’d first need to define what the benchmark aims to measure (“ability to resolve flagged issues in software,” for instance), break that into subskills (different types of problems or types of program that the AI model can successfully process), and then finally assemble questions that accurately cover the different subskills.

It’s a profound change from how AI researchers typically approach benchmarking—but for researchers like Jacobs, a coauthor on the February paper, that’s the whole point. “There’s a mismatch between what’s happening in the tech industry and these tools from social science,” she says. “We have decades and decades of thinking about how we want to measure these squishy things about humans.”

Even though the idea has made a real impact in the research world, it’s been slow to influence the way AI companies are actually using benchmarks. 

The last two months have seen new model releases from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta, and all of them lean heavily on multiple-choice knowledge benchmarks like MMLU—the exact approach that validity researchers are trying to move past. After all, model releases are, for the most part, still about showing increases in general intelligence, and broad benchmarks continue to be used to back up those claims. 

For some observers, that’s good enough. Benchmarks, Wharton professor Ethan Mollick says, are “bad measures of things, but also they’re what we’ve got.” He adds: “At the same time, the models are getting better. A lot of sins are forgiven by fast progress.”

For now, the industry’s long-standing focus on artificial general intelligence seems to be crowding out a more focused validity-based approach. As long as AI models can keep growing in general intelligence, then specific applications don’t seem as compelling—even if that leaves practitioners relying on tools they no longer fully trust. 

“This is the tightrope we’re walking,” says Hugging Face’s Solaiman. “It’s too easy to throw the system out, but evaluations are really helpful in understanding our models, even with these limitations.”

Russell Brandom is a freelance writer covering artificial intelligence. He lives in Brooklyn with his wife and two cats.
