text:
📜 THIS DAY IN DIPLOMATIC HISTORY
        November 12, 1921

An American secretary of state rose to open a disarmament conference and proposed to send nearly seventy warships to the breakers at a stroke, close to two million tons of fighting ships. The admirals in the room were appalled. One of them looked, a watching journalist wrote, like a bulldog kicked awake on his own doorstep. It was the first time great powers ever agreed to destroy their own weapons by treaty.

On November 12, 1921, the Washington Conference on the Limitation of Armament opened in the American capital. Its sessions were declared public, the speeches printed in the newspapers the same day, and the press announced that the age of secret diplomacy was over and that the whole world was watching. Fourteen delegations took their seats, the British dominions and India counting as separate powers. The United States was led by its secretary of state, Charles Evans Hughes, who was also chosen to chair the conference. Britain sent Arthur Balfour, France its premier, Aristide Briand, Japan the former foreign minister, Baron Katō.

Speaking first, Hughes laid out exact numbers on behalf of the American government. The powers should stop building the great capital ships at once, scrap a long list of existing and half-built vessels named one by one, and then hold their battle fleets to fixed tonnage ceilings. He proposed a ten-year holiday in new construction. He named the ships Britain and Japan and America would each have to send to the breakers.  When he said aloud that Britain must halt work on her newest battleships, the British admiral Lord Beatty leaned forward in his chair, the journalist Mark Sullivan recorded, like a dozing bulldog that an impudent passer-by had just kicked.

The daring proposal landed because it suited nearly everyone. Britain had built a vast war fleet she could no longer afford, and was deep in debt, so cutting ships was a relief she welcomed. Three days later Balfour announced that Britain accepted Hughes's plan in principle, and read out a telegram of praise from the prime minister, David Lloyd George. Japan's Baron Katō agreed in principle too. Briand accepted for France, but added that what France truly cared about was limiting armies on land, not ships at sea.

The unanimity was a courtesy, and it cracked the moment the talk turned from principle to numbers. Hughes wanted the battle fleets fixed in a settled proportion, with Britain and the United States equal at the top and Japan held below them. The ratio came out as five to five to three. Japan refused it, demanding ten to ten to seven instead. The Americans threatened to lay down four ships for every one the Japanese built. Japan then gave way on the figures, but only on one condition: that the United States build no new naval bases in the western Pacific, leaving Guam and the Philippines unfortified. For the smaller battle fleets of France and Italy, Hughes offered a tonnage of 175,000 each. The French, resentful at being ranked so far below, at last accepted rather than wreck the conference.

France had come in a sour mood from the start. At the opening session no place had been found for Briand at the central table, every seat taken by Americans and Englishmen, and the French premier had to sit off to one side until the end. His delegation read it, fairly enough, as a slight to French prestige. The deeper quarrel was over land armies. Britain said it would disarm at sea only if France first cut its great army on land, a manoeuvre that neatly set Paris and Washington against each other. Briand refused, declaring that no people longed for peace more fervently than France, and that the army was needed to save Poland and all of Western Europe from the Bolsheviks. The question of land armies was handed to a committee, where it quietly died. The conference limited ships. It never touched a single soldier.

Out of Washington came a string of treaties. On December 13, 1921, the four Pacific powers, the United States, Britain, Japan and France, signed the Four-Power Treaty, pledging to respect one another's island possessions in the Pacific. Buried in its text was the real American prize. On ratification, the Anglo-Japanese Alliance of 1902 would lapse. British diplomats insisted it was not cancelled but merely replaced, yet a Japanese delegate put the truth more plainly, telling his British counterpart that they had given the alliance a splendid funeral. Washington had quietly severed the bond between London and Tokyo. The naval ratios were sealed on February 6, 1922, in the Five-Power Treaty, with capital-ship tonnage fixed at 525,000 for the United States, the same for Britain, 315,000 for Japan, and 175,000 each for France and Italy.

Two of the powers most concerned were kept from the table, and one of them came anyway. Soviet Russia had not been invited, and Washington did not even recognise it, but it refused to be ignored at a conference redrawing the balance of power along its own eastern coast. It sent a delegation in the name of the Far Eastern Republic, the buffer state at Chita that Moscow quietly controlled. Hughes received the delegates but would not seat them. Their errand was to demand that Japan at last withdraw its army from Siberia, where it had been entrenched since the civil war. Denied a hearing, the delegation struck back in the newspapers, publishing documents it said proved a secret deal between Japan and France to build a Japanese sphere in the Far East. Japan and France denounced the papers as forgeries, and their authenticity was never settled, but the leak embarrassed Tokyo and helped force the Siberian question onto the conference floor. Japan would evacuate the Siberian mainland the following year.

China too was present, yet the powers settled the affairs of the Far East largely over its head. And the bargain that bought Japan's signature, the promise to leave the western Pacific unfortified, handed Tokyo naval supremacy in its own waters. The Washington system kept the peace for a decade. Then Japan walked away from it, as Germany had walked away from Geneva, and the unfortified bases and the three-to-five ratio that Japan had never forgiven led, in time, toward Pearl Harbor.

text:
Watch Clyde Drexler collect a rebound and start running.

The first few strides tell you why “The Glide” fit so perfectly. He covered ground with a smoothness that could disguise how quickly a defense was running out of time.

Retreat toward the basket, and he could keep coming. Step into his path, and he could find the teammate your rotation had left open.

The dunk usually made the highlight. The decision that created it deserved just as much attention.

Drexler was a scorer who could rebound like a forward and turn immediately into a playmaker. That versatility helped make Portland one of the most dangerous teams of its era.

He led the Blazers to the Finals in 1990 and 1992.

Then Houston revealed another dimension of his greatness.

Joining Hakeem Olajuwon meant fitting his talents around an established championship centerpiece. Drexler gave the Rockets another player who could attack the basket, create a shot and keep a possession moving when the defense crowded Hakeem.

During Houston’s 1995 championship run, he averaged 20.5 points, 7.0 rebounds and 5.0 assists across 22 playoff games.

That is substantial production for a player whose contribution sometimes gets compressed into “Hakeem finally had help.”

Drexler brought the experience of leading a contender and the versatility to strengthen someone else’s.

Houston entered those playoffs as the sixth seed and finished as champion. Clyde’s ability to influence the game in several ways was essential to that journey.

His career offers a useful reminder about greatness: a player can carry enormous responsibility, share it effectively and remain unmistakably himself.

In Portland, Drexler helped establish the standard.

In Houston, he helped finish the job.

And wherever he played, the defense had better start retreating when he grabbed that rebound.

text:
I wanted to keep this creature in the series even though we do not have a proper name for it. The underwater encounter in the Absolute Wonder Woman annual is part of Diana's journey, and an unnamed creature is still a creature worth noticing. Calling it a Kraken just to fill in the blank would make the description less accurate.

Spoilers for the Absolute Wonder Woman 2026 Annual.

The comic gives us an aquatic monster and a confrontation, but not a developed origin or a complete account of its abilities. We have not been given a secure species name or a reason to identify it with one specific famous sea monster.

That matters when talking about powers. An underwater appearance does not establish unlimited depth tolerance, control of the sea, regeneration, or a magical connection with Poseidon. Those would need their own evidence. For now, its place in the story is as a creature Diana encounters in an environment very different from the land around her.

Greek mythology has a broad tradition of sea monsters called ketea, with ketos as the singular. The word does not describe one tightly defined species with a fixed anatomy. It is more useful to think about the role of the monstrous sea creature in the story than to imagine an ancient zoological classification.

The monster associated with Andromeda is one well-known example. In the tradition preserved by Apollodorus, Cassiopeia's boast about beauty angers the Nereids. Poseidon sends disaster and a sea monster, and Andromeda is exposed to the creature as the proposed price of ending the suffering. Perseus encounters her and kills the monster.

That story gives the creature a divine function. It is a danger emerging from the sea, but the reason it arrives is bound up with a conflict between human pride and divine authority. Andromeda ends up paying for a dispute she did not begin.

There is another sea-monster story at Troy involving Hesione and Heracles. King Laomedon's dealings with the gods bring disaster to his city. Hesione is offered to the monster, and Heracles agrees to rescue her in return for a promised reward. After he defeats the creature, Laomedon's failure to honor the agreement leads to further conflict.

The two stories share a recognizable situation, but they are not the same event. Different people, grievances, and promises are involved. That is another reason not to take every creature rising from the water and assume it must be the monster from Andromeda's story.

The sea gives these encounters a particular kind of uncertainty. On land, a person can see a body approaching across a field. Water can hide most of the body, distort its outline, and leave people on shore waiting for something they cannot fully see. Ancient storytellers had a great deal to work with before adding any divine punishment at all.

The Kraken belongs to a different, northern European tradition. Using that name for every large aquatic monster can erase the differences between traditions as well as the differences between fictional characters. A resemblance is not an identification.

For Absolute, the honest place to stop is with the unnamed encounter. The Greek sea-monster tradition gives us a rich background for it, but the annual has not told us that this creature is Poseidon's punishment, Andromeda's monster, or a survivor of Heracles's adventures. Diana's world is large enough to contain beings whose whole history we have not been told yet.

text:
Petra is another character where I wanted to go further than the name of the creature. She is a siren, she has a dangerous voice, and she has wings. But when Diana first encounters her, she is the one who needs help. Ferdinand has been protecting her inside the maze, and her condition is serious enough that getting her out becomes an immediate priority.

Spoilers for Absolute Wonder Woman.

Petra appears alongside Ferdinand in #9, and the escape through the next few issues shows how dependent she has become on him for safety. Clea's forces are pursuing them. Petra is weak and largely silent during this part of the story, so we meet her before we get a full demonstration of the ability people would associate with a siren.

Diana gets her through the portal ahead of the others in #10. That removes her from the maze, but she is now in an unfamiliar place without Ferdinand. By #12, her siren wail has immobilized the people around her at the Hieron. Her voice is capable of affecting multiple listeners, and being out of the prison has not automatically made her feel safe.

Ferdinand reaches her and talks to her. He reassures her that he is there and that they are free, and the reunion ends the crisis. So the scene gives us a very specific use of her vocal power during fear and distress. It does not require us to assume she deliberately planned to attack the people who rescued her.

Her appearance also matters when we compare her with older siren traditions. Petra has wings, sharp teeth, and a humanlike face and upper body. The familiar modern habit of picturing every siren as a mermaid would give the wrong impression here. Wings have a much older place in siren imagery than a lot of people realize.

The demonstrated vocal effect is the main supernatural ability I would put at the center of her profile. It can disable a group, and calming her changes what happens. The comic does not give us a precise range, establish that every listener can always resist it the same way, or show that she can order people to do absolutely anything. Her condition also makes it clear that having a powerful voice does not make her impossible to injure or leave helpless.

There is a long history behind those voices. In Homer's Odyssey, Circe warns Odysseus about the Sirens before he reaches them. Anyone who approaches and listens risks never returning to his family. The Sirens sit in a meadow surrounded by the remains of people who have already been drawn in.

What they offer Odysseus is especially interesting. They call him by name and promise knowledge. They say they know what happened at Troy and what happens across the world. The attraction in that scene includes the chance to hear things he wants to know, including the story of the war he has just survived. Reducing them to creatures who tempt men with physical beauty misses what Homer actually puts into their song.

Odysseus wants to hear it, so he follows Circe's instructions. His sailors block their ears with wax, while he is tied upright to the mast. He tells them beforehand that if he begs to be released, they should bind him more tightly. When the song reaches him, that is exactly the safeguard he needs. He wants to go toward it, and the crew keep rowing until they have passed beyond hearing.

That is a very practical response to a supernatural danger. The sailors prevent themselves from receiving the sound at all. Odysseus allows himself to hear it but removes his ability to act on what it makes him want. He does not defeat the Sirens in a singing contest or suddenly become immune through determination. He survives through preparation and people who keep following his earlier instructions when his wishes change.

The Argonautica gives us another approach. Orpheus plays his lyre when the Argonauts come near the Sirens, filling their ears with his own music and overcoming the song. Butes still leaps overboard, overcome by what he hears, and Aphrodite rescues him. So even that escape has a near-failure. The story gives the Sirens a countermeasure without making their power harmless.

The birdlike anatomy is clearer in ancient art and in writers after Homer. Homer does not stop to describe a complete body design in the Odyssey. Apollonius describes beings that are partly women and partly birds, and Ovid gives them human faces with the feet and feathers of birds. Petra's wings fit into that older tradition even though her personal history belongs to the comic.

Their connection to Persephone adds another layer. In Ovid's Metamorphoses, the Sirens were her companions. After she disappeared, they searched for her on land and wanted wings so they could continue searching over the sea. Their transformation preserves their human faces and voices. In that telling, the wings answer a desire to find someone they have lost.

Hyginus preserves a harsher version: Demeter gives them bird forms because they failed to help her daughter. That changes the transformation from assistance with a search into punishment for not preventing an abduction. Both versions belong to the older tradition, but they are not the same explanation. Neither establishes that Petra personally served Persephone or was transformed by Demeter.

The family details differ as well. Achelous, the river god, is often their father, while different sources give them different mothers, including Muses. Apollonius names Terpsichore. That connects their extraordinary music with a divine musical family, but ancient writers do not supply one universally agreed list of names, parents, and numbers for all Sirens.

There is also a real connection with mourning. Sirens appear on ancient Greek funerary monuments, sometimes playing instruments or making gestures of grief. The Walters Art Museum has a fourth-century BC siren with a kithara that originally stood on a grave monument. The Met also has examples associated with the afterlife. In that setting, their song can be understood as lamentation rather than the lure that endangers sailors.

That wider history is worth keeping alongside the dangerous-song stories. Sirens were connected with irresistible knowledge, music, loss, the search for Persephone, and mourning for the dead. Petra does not have to inherit every one of those stories for the comparison to be useful. Her own scene centers on somebody frightened enough that her power becomes dangerous, and the person she trusts coming back to her. Ferdinand understands who she is even when everyone else is experiencing what her voice can do.

“Where is the bread going?”

I said, “I was about to ask you.”

She went quiet. Then she turned her monitor around.

Security footage. 10:40pm. The loading dock.

It was her, in her coat, carrying my bags to her own car.

“I grew up in Tulsa,” she said. “Some nights my mom and I ate what the bakery down the street couldn’t sell.”

“Corporate says anything unsold gets tossed. Legal says donating is a liability. So I’ve been driving it to the church pantry on 11th Street myself. 4 nights a week. For 2 years.”

Nobody had noticed. Except me, at 10pm.

The next morning I called the food bank. They’d already offered to pick up from stores for free. She’d just never been allowed to say yes.

She sent the request up the chain that afternoon.

Now the cage by the loading dock has a new label: “Unsold bread: food bank pickup, Tuesdays and Fridays.”

The other 3 nights, she still takes it herself.

Taped above the cage, in her handwriting:

“Not trash. Ignore the log.”

text: Tales from a preachers daughter. Remember, I grew up on the beach. We had a police department. But they always looked away. So people cooked meth in their kitchens, had lions and tigers (let your imagination run wild there).  I lived in what they call upscale Houston that day-  since 4 years old. Dad decided to stop being a police offer and went full on preacher mode. What we could not fit in one U-Haul  is what arrived. Dad wasn’t going back. So me and my older sister had our beds. My mom and dad, too. Table kitchen and some extras thrown in. A cabinet for the tv. I recall being 4 and leaving it all on the curb for people to pick up. I’m 4 mind you, and driving to the beach. We are in my mom’s Lincoln Mercy and I’m crying in leather seats. No please, I want to go back home. Mom did her best to reassure me. I walked in to what was to be my bedroom with this thing in the window of my a Glassdoor. It was the office of previous owners. So I had “office” written on my Glassdoor for years. Zero privacy. Then it was the ac unit hanging from a window. “What is this? Can we go back now mom. I promise I’ll be good”. The house had no female touch and smelled like the ocean and withering seafood.  We stayed. I managed. Then when times got too tough, mom had to sell her beloved leather seat car to the neighbor that trashed it. She would look out the window everyday of our bathroom and see her car there, that’s a lot for a woman . Omg. I just remember staring with her. What strength she had. It was something like this. Not exactly. But she shined in all her glory and we had to sell her to the neighbor- of all people. So she saw it every single day from the bathroom window. Omg. I can’t.

Tesla's Robotaxi Expansion: Is Elon Musk Finally Turning Autonomous Driving Into a Scalable Business?

The race to commercialize autonomous transportation is accelerating as Tesla expands its Robotaxi operations across major American cities, including Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, San Antonio, Miami, Orlando, and Tampa.

Recent reports suggest Tesla is approaching round-the-clock operations in some markets, signaling a transition from limited deployments toward a more ambitious commercial transportation network.

The real breakthrough will not simply be removing the human driver. It will be proving that autonomous vehicles can operate safely, reliably, and profitably at scale.

Tesla's strategy differs significantly from traditional ride-hailing services. Rather than relying on human drivers, the company aims to combine AI-powered driving systems, electric vehicles, fleet management, and automated operations.

Its purpose-built Cybercab represents an important component of that vision, potentially allowing Tesla to improve vehicle utilization while reducing operating costs.

However, fleet size alone does not establish competitive leadership. The critical measures include paid rides, passenger miles, vehicle utilization, intervention rates, safety performance, and operating profitability.

A fleet of autonomous vehicles creates economic value only when those vehicles consistently transport paying customers safely and efficiently.

My perspective is that Tesla's greatest opportunity lies in the economics of transportation.

Traditional ride-hailing platforms must compensate human drivers, while autonomous networks could eventually reduce that expense. Yet vehicle depreciation, maintenance, insurance, charging, remote assistance, and regulatory compliance remain substantial costs.

Competition with Waymo will increasingly test which technology can deliver dependable service across different cities, traffic conditions, and operating environments.

The autonomous driving race is shifting from impressive demonstrations toward measurable business performance.

Importantly, expanding operating hours does not establish that every city offers unrestricted 24/7 service. Tesla's own guidance indicates availability varies by location, while its Bay Area operations continue to involve human drivers.

For investors, the important question is whether expansion can translate into sustainable revenue without compromising passenger safety.

If Tesla successfully scales autonomous transportation, the implications could extend across urban mobility, insurance, logistics, vehicle ownership, and the economics of transportation.

The future of Robotaxi will not be determined by who deploys the most vehicles, but by who creates the safest, most reliable, and economically sustainable autonomous transportation network.

5. Isotopes trace Ancestral Pueblo azurite across the Southwest
Researchers measured lead, strontium and copper isotopes in 12 Ancestral Pueblo azurite objects. Ten—including all nine spherical or partial-spherical specimens—were linked to Lisbon Valley in Utah; two irregular pieces were attributed to New Mexico’s Zuni Mountains.

Established evidence: Lead and strontium signatures reliably distinguished the two tested sources. Copper isotopes did not.

Uncertainty: Twelve objects and two geological comparison areas constitute a limited source map. The findings show material movement by roughly AD 600, but not whether every object was acquired through direct travel.

Why it matters: The research offers a replicable way to examine traditional territories and exchange without automatically turning long-distance material circulation into evidence of state control.

Source: “Spheres of Blue: Isotopic evidence for the provenance of azurite in the Ancestral Pueblo world” — Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports, September 22, 2026 • https://t.co/siv94LThHR

text:
Must read book for every indian-
How did a girl from a small village in Italy rise as a politician in India and become known around the world? 
Belonging begins in Cambridge, England, where in 1965 Sonia Maino, a nineteen-year-old student, falls in love at first sight with the handsome young man she's destined to marry: Rajiv Gandhi, grandson of Jawaharlal Nehru, independent India's first Prime Minister. 
In this book, the once famously reticent Sonia Gandhi opens up with warmth and candour to narrate the story of her remarkable life, from her childhood in post-war Italy to the romance that brings her to India and the shattering losses that will reshape not only her own future but also that of her adopted home. 
We witness Sonia's introduction to her formidable mother-in-law, Nehru's daughter, Indira Gandhi, India's first female Prime Minister. We see Sonia gain confidence by Rajiv's side as she adjusts to the sounds and sights of her new home --- learning to speak Hindi, to wear saris, to relish spicy cuisine. 
Rajiv Gandhi begins work as a commercial airline pilot, and they raise their two children in the Prime Minister's house in New Delhi. But everything changes when Rajiv's brother, Sanjay, also a pilot, is killed in a plane crash, and when, in 1984, Indira Gandhi is brutally assassinated by her security guards in the garden of her home. In the wake of his mother's death, and despite Sonia's fears, Rajiv steps into the role of Prime Minister. Then, through Sonia's wrenching retelling, we feel the full force of the tragedy when seven years later Rajiv, too, is assassinated by a suicide bomber while on the campaign trail. 
For several years Sonia resists the pressure to join politics, but ultimately accepts the challenge, becoming the longest-serving president of the Indian National Congress. We see how, though once regarded as a foreign-born outsider, she comes to earn the trust and affection of millions. Yet, when after a key election, the Congress Party selects her to become Prime Minister, she makes the surprising decision to decline the country's highest office, and chooses instead to lead her party in an alliance that will govern India for a decade. 
This dramatic account, epic and intimate, gives readers a unique lens on India --- its tumultuous post-Independence history and its present political struggles --- offering an insider's keen perspective on the country's enormous political, economic and social changes over sixty years. Most moving of all is the portrait of Sonia herself that emerges as she invites readers into her private joys and travails, and offers glimpses of the people and events that have shaped her. In a voice at once perceptive and modest, she shares her insights into identity, duty and the meaning of home. Belonging is at heart one courageous woman's story of falling in love with a man and a country, and of finding the place where she belongs.

text:
$TWT — THE $166 MILLION SELF-CUSTODY BET
⠀
One of crypto's most recognizable self-custody wallets.
⠀
A token with a fixed supply of approximately 1 BILLION.
⠀
A growing ecosystem of swaps, trading, rewards, and AI-powered wallet services.
⠀
And a new strategy designed to connect wallet activity with token demand.
⠀
But here's the contradiction.
⠀
Trust Wallet can grow its user base.
⠀
Trading volume can increase.
⠀
More assets can flow through its ecosystem.
⠀
Yet TWT holders do not automatically receive the profits generated by those activities.
⠀
At approximately $0.385, TWT carries a market capitalization near $166 million.
⠀
Is $TWT an overlooked consumer crypto infrastructure asset?
⠀
Or is the market correctly discounting a token whose economic value depends on the success of a new utility model?
⠀
Let's examine the fundamentals.
⠀
01 | WHAT IS TRUST WALLET TOKEN?
⠀
TWT is the native utility token associated with Trust Wallet.
⠀
Trust Wallet is a self-custody cryptocurrency wallet that allows users to manage digital assets without surrendering control of their private keys to the wallet provider.
⠀
Its ecosystem includes:
⠀
• Multi-chain asset management
• Crypto swaps
• Fiat on-ramps
• DeFi integrations
• Trading services
• Trust Premium
• Trust Alpha rewards
• AI-powered wallet features
⠀
The investment thesis centers on converting wallet usage into demand for TWT.
⠀
But platform adoption and token value capture are separate questions.
⠀
02 | THE NUMBERS THAT MATTER
⠀
TWT Price: ~$0.385
⠀
Market Cap: ~$165.6M
⠀
Fully Diluted Valuation: ~$385.1M
⠀
Circulating Supply: ~429.86M TWT
⠀
Maximum Supply: ~999.86M TWT
⠀
Circulating Ratio: ~43.0%
⠀
24H Trading Volume: ~$4.0M
⠀
Historical ATH: ~$2.72
⠀
Current Price vs ATH: ~86% Below
⠀
These figures reflect the November 12, 2026 market snapshot using CoinMarketCap supply estimates.
⠀
The most important observation?
⠀
Less than half of the maximum supply is classified as circulating.
⠀
That makes future token distribution a major part of the valuation equation.
⠀
03 | THE SELF-CUSTODY OPPORTUNITY
⠀
Self-custody allows users to control their own cryptocurrency assets.
⠀
Unlike centralized exchange accounts, self-custody wallets give users direct control over their private keys.
⠀
This creates demand for:
⠀
Secure asset storage.
⠀
Cross-chain transfers.
⠀
Token swaps.
⠀
DeFi access.
⠀
And integrated financial services.
⠀
Trust Wallet is positioned within this market.
⠀
But the growth of self-custody does not automatically create TWT demand.
⠀
Most wallet functions can be used without holding the token.
⠀
04 | THE TOKENOMICS REDESIGN
⠀
Trust Wallet published a revised TWT utility strategy in September 2025.
⠀
The goal was to connect token ownership more closely with product usage and user loyalty.
⠀
The framework includes:
⠀
Token locking.
⠀
Tiered benefits.
⠀
Transaction fee discounts.
⠀
Reward opportunities.
⠀
Premium services.
⠀
And additional utility integrations.
⠀
This is an important strategic change.
⠀
But investors must distinguish between proposed features and benefits that are already operational.
⠀
A roadmap is not proof of economic demand.
⠀
05 | THE TRUST PREMIUM MODEL
⠀
Trust Premium is designed as a loyalty system connected to wallet activity.
⠀
Users can participate through eligible actions such as swaps and other supported activities.
⠀
TWT locking can enhance certain benefits.
⠀
This creates a potential incentive to hold tokens rather than immediately sell them.
⠀
But the economic impact depends on:
⠀
Active participants.
⠀
TWT locked.
⠀
Lock duration.
⠀
Reward costs.
⠀
And recurring user engagement.
⠀
A loyalty program creates token demand only when users value the benefits enough to acquire and retain TWT.
⠀
06 | THE TRUST ALPHA OPPORTUNITY
⠀
Trust Alpha connects eligible wallet users with early-stage projects and reward opportunities.
⠀
Certain programs have required users to lock TWT and complete qualifying wallet activities.
⠀
This creates a practical use case for the token.
⠀
But reward programs can attract temporary capital.
⠀
Users may lock TWT for incentives and sell after rewards are distributed.
⠀
The important metric is sustained token retention after campaigns end.
⠀
A successful promotional campaign is not the same as permanent economic demand.
⠀
07 | THE FEE DISCOUNT THESIS
⠀
Trust Wallet's token strategy includes fee discounts linked to TWT utility.
⠀
Potential benefits involve swaps and selected financial services.
⠀
This could create a relationship between trading activity and token holding.
⠀
But investors should ask:
⠀
How much are users actually saving?
⠀
How much TWT must they hold?
⠀
What is the average holding period?
⠀
And do the savings justify the token's price volatility?
⠀
A discount token becomes valuable when the economic benefit is meaningful and recurring.
⠀
08 | THE FLEXGAS INTEGRATION
⠀
Trust Wallet introduced FlexGas functionality that supports paying certain transaction fees with assets including TWT.
⠀
This improves user convenience by reducing the need to maintain separate native gas-token balances for supported transactions.
⠀
But paying fees with TWT does not necessarily mean TWT is the underlying network's native gas asset.
⠀
The actual settlement and conversion mechanism matters.
⠀
Investors should distinguish payment convenience from permanent token consumption.
⠀
A token can be useful for payments without creating lasting buying pressure.
⠀
09 | THE TOKEN SUPPLY PROBLEM
⠀
TWT has a fixed total supply of approximately 1 billion tokens.
⠀
The official litepaper states that the token contract does not permit new minting.
⠀
However, fixed supply does not mean all tokens are already circulating.
⠀
CoinMarketCap reports approximately 429.86 million circulating TWT.
⠀
That leaves roughly 570 million tokens outside its circulating-supply classification.
⠀
These tokens are not necessarily scheduled for immediate release.
⠀
But investors must understand their ownership, restrictions, and distribution plans.
⠀
The absence of new minting does not eliminate future circulating-supply dilution.
⠀
10 | THE REMAINING ALLOCATIONS
⠀
Trust Wallet's litepaper identifies several purposes for remaining noncirculating allocations.
⠀
These include:
⠀
Future ecosystem growth.
⠀
Liquidity programs.
⠀
Strategic partnerships.
⠀
And core team incentives.
⠀
Such allocations can support long-term development.
⠀
But they also introduce potential future selling pressure.
⠀
The relevant questions are:
⠀
When can tokens become liquid?
⠀
Who controls them?
⠀
How are distributions approved?
⠀
And how much reaches exchanges?
⠀
Without a reliable release schedule, investors should not invent unlock dates.
⠀
11 | THE WALLET REVENUE QUESTION
⠀
Trust Wallet offers multiple services that may generate commercial revenue.
⠀
These include trading-related features, integrations, and other wallet services.
⠀
But company revenue is not automatically TWT tokenholder revenue.
⠀
TWT is not equity in Trust Wallet.
⠀
Holding TWT does not create an automatic contractual claim on company profits.
⠀
Investors should distinguish:
⠀
Wallet transaction volume.
⠀
Company revenue.
⠀
Partner revenue.
⠀
TWT-related fee payments.
⠀
And direct tokenholder economic benefits.
⠀
Only verified economic links should be included in a token valuation.
⠀
12 | THE AI WALLET EXPANSION
⠀
Trust Wallet introduced AI-focused products in 2026.
⠀
These include Trust Wallet AI and infrastructure for autonomous agents.
⠀
AI agents may increasingly require tools to hold assets, execute transactions, and interact with blockchain networks.
⠀
This creates an interesting distribution opportunity.
⠀
But the AI narrative requires caution.
⠀
More AI-powered wallet activity does not automatically increase TWT demand.
⠀
The relevant question is whether these services require TWT or create meaningful benefits for holders.
⠀
Without that connection, AI adoption primarily strengthens the wallet product.
⠀
13 | THE COMPETITIVE LANDSCAPE
⠀
Trust Wallet competes with:
⠀
• MetaMask
• Phantom
• Coinbase Wallet
• Rabby
• Other multi-chain wallets
⠀
Competition is intense.
⠀
Wallets compete on security, supported chains, transaction costs, usability, and integrated financial services.
⠀
Switching costs can be relatively low for users who manage multiple wallets.
⠀
Trust Wallet must retain users through superior functionality.
⠀
TWT must separately demonstrate why those users should hold its token.
⠀
14 | THE SECURITY RISK
⠀
Self-custody reduces dependence on centralized custodians.
⠀
But it introduces different risks.
⠀
Users can lose funds through:
⠀
Seed phrase exposure.
⠀
Malicious approvals.
⠀
Phishing.
⠀
Compromised devices.
⠀
And vulnerable integrations.
⠀
A security incident can damage confidence in the wallet ecosystem.
⠀
But holding TWT does not provide insurance against wallet losses.
⠀
Investors should not confuse self-custody with risk-free custody.
⠀
15 | THE HISTORICAL PRICE QUESTION
⠀
TWT previously reached approximately $2.72.
⠀
At around $0.385, it trades roughly 86% below that peak.
⠀
That may attract investors looking for recovery opportunities.
⠀
But a large drawdown is not evidence of undervaluation.
⠀
Token distribution, market conditions, and competitive dynamics have changed.
⠀
The relevant question is whether current and future TWT demand can justify a higher valuation.
⠀
Historical prices are not reliable investment targets.
⠀
16 | THE VALUATION FRAMEWORK
⠀
Using approximately 1 billion TWT as the maximum supply:
⠀
$0.25 implies ~$250M FDV.
⠀
$0.50 implies ~$500M.
⠀
$1.00 implies ~$1B.
⠀
$2.00 implies ~$2B.
⠀
$3.00 implies ~$3B.
⠀
$5.00 implies ~$5B.
⠀
These are illustrative valuations, not price targets.
⠀
At $1, TWT would carry a fully diluted valuation near $1 billion.
⠀
That is significantly above its current FDV of approximately $385 million.
⠀
Such a revaluation would require stronger token demand, higher market expectations, or both.
⠀
A successful wallet alone does not justify that valuation.
⠀
17 | THE BULL CASE
⠀
TWT could benefit if:
⠀
Self-custody adoption accelerates.
⠀
Trust Wallet attracts more active traders.
⠀
Trust Premium participation grows.
⠀
Users lock more TWT for benefits.
⠀
Trust Alpha rewards encourage long-term holding.
⠀
Fee discounts create recurring demand.
⠀
And wallet activity becomes more directly connected to token utility.
⠀
Under this scenario, TWT could evolve into a more important consumer crypto loyalty asset.
⠀
But the investment thesis requires measurable token participation.
⠀
18 | THE BEAR CASE
⠀
The bearish scenario is equally important.
⠀
Trust Wallet grows without increasing TWT adoption.
⠀
Competing wallets offer similar services without requiring a token.
⠀
Rewards attract short-term participants.
⠀
Noncirculating tokens enter the market.
⠀
Fee discounts fail to justify holding TWT.
⠀
And wallet revenue remains economically separate from tokenholder value.
⠀
Under this scenario, Trust Wallet could remain successful while TWT underperforms.
⠀
19 | THE FINAL VERDICT
⠀
TWT has several important strengths.
⠀
An established self-custody wallet ecosystem.
⠀
A fixed maximum supply.
⠀
Real utility through selected wallet features.
⠀
A developing loyalty and rewards framework.
⠀
And exposure to growing on-chain financial activity.
⠀
But here's the contradiction.
⠀
A recognizable wallet brand.
⠀
A token designed to reward ecosystem participation.
⠀
And a strategy to connect product usage with token holding.
⠀
Yet less than half the supply is classified as circulating, while direct token value capture remains difficult to quantify.
⠀
The next major catalyst isn't simply another wallet integration.
⠀
It's evidence that more active users are acquiring and locking TWT because the benefits justify holding it.
⠀
Wallet adoption demonstrates distribution.
⠀
Trading activity demonstrates usage.
⠀
Token locking demonstrates participation.
⠀
But sustainable net demand determines long-term investment value.
⠀
The market isn't just asking whether Trust Wallet can grow.
⠀
It's asking whether that growth will create enough economic demand for TWT.
⠀
Bookmark this analysis before the next wallet infrastructure rotation.
⠀
Which has the strongest long-term wallet token thesis?
⠀
$TWT, $SAFE, or $C98?
⠀
And can Trust Wallet convert its consumer distribution into sustainable token demand?
⠀
Drop your view below.
⠀

Or is the market correctly discounting its dependence on Curve, liquidity incentives, and governance demand?

Let's examine the fundamentals.

01 | WHAT IS CONVEX FINANCE?
⠀
Convex Finance is a DeFi protocol designed to optimize rewards and governance participation across supported liquidity ecosystems.
⠀
Its original strategy focused on Curve Finance.
⠀
Convex aggregates deposits and voting power to improve reward opportunities for participating users.
⠀
Its ecosystem includes:
⠀
• Curve liquidity optimization
• cvxCRV
• CVX staking
• Vote-locked CVX
• Gauge voting
• Governance incentives
• Additional supported DeFi integrations
⠀
Convex is not a conventional lending protocol.
⠀
Its competitive advantage comes from coordinating liquidity incentives and governance power.
⠀
02 | THE NUMBERS THAT MATTER
⠀
CVX Price: ~$1.73
⠀
Market Cap: ~$160.8M
⠀
Fully Diluted Valuation: ~$172.5M
⠀

⠀

These figures represent the November 12, 2026 research snapshot.
⠀
The most important distinction?
⠀
Reported holders revenue is not equivalent to an automatic cash dividend paid to every CVX holder.
⠀
03 | THE CURVE CONNECTION
⠀
Curve Finance is an important decentralized exchange ecosystem, particularly for stablecoin and correlated-asset liquidity.
⠀
Curve uses voting mechanisms to influence how token incentives are allocated among liquidity pools.
⠀
Convex aggregates governance power and provides services built around that system.
⠀
This creates a potentially valuable position.
⠀
Projects seeking liquidity may have an incentive to influence reward allocations.
⠀
But Convex's economics remain heavily exposed to the health and competitiveness of the underlying ecosystems.
⠀
04 | THE YIELD OPTIMIZATION MODEL
⠀
Convex allows participating liquidity providers to access reward optimization without individually managing every aspect of Curve governance.
⠀
The protocol coordinates deposits and reward mechanisms.
⠀
This can simplify the user experience.
⠀
But yield optimization is not risk-free.
⠀
Users remain exposed to underlying assets, smart contracts, market volatility, and liquidity conditions.
⠀
Higher displayed yields do not automatically imply higher risk-adjusted returns.
⠀
05 | THE CVXCRV ECONOMY
⠀
cvxCRV represents tokenized exposure to CRV deposited and locked through Convex.
⠀
Users can participate in reward mechanisms through cvxCRV.
⠀
But cvxCRV should not be treated as identical to liquid CRV.
⠀
Its market price can diverge from CRV.
⠀
Liquidity conditions and redemption limitations matter.
⠀
A reward-bearing token can carry substantial basis risk even when its underlying exposure appears familiar.
⠀
06 | THE CVX TOKEN UTILITY
⠀
CVX is the native token of Convex Finance.
⠀
Its principal functions include:
⠀
Governance participation.
⠀
Vote locking.
⠀
Influence over gauge allocations.
⠀
Access to protocol-related rewards.
⠀
And participation in the broader incentive economy.
⠀
Unlike governance tokens with no implemented reward mechanism, CVX has established staking and locking arrangements.
⠀
But the value of these arrangements depends on actual rewards, market liquidity, and governance demand.
⠀
07 | THE VLCVX MECHANISM
⠀
CVX holders can lock tokens to participate in governance.
⠀
The standard vote-locking period is approximately 16 weeks, with timing affected by the weekly epoch schedule.
⠀
Locked CVX can influence voting decisions and receive applicable rewards.
⠀
This creates an economic incentive to lock supply.
⠀
But locking introduces liquidity risk.
⠀
Holders cannot freely exit during the lock period.
⠀
If CVX falls sharply, reward income may be insufficient to offset capital losses.
⠀
08 | THE CURVE WARS
⠀
The term Curve Wars describes competition for influence over liquidity incentives.
⠀
Projects want their liquidity pools to receive attractive rewards.
⠀
Governance power can influence how those incentives are distributed.
⠀
Convex became important because it aggregates substantial voting influence.
⠀
This creates demand for governance participation.
⠀
But the economic value of voting power depends on the willingness of external projects to compete for it.
⠀
If incentive budgets shrink, governance-related revenue can decline.
⠀
09 | THE VOTING INCENTIVE ECONOMY
⠀
External projects may offer incentives to participants who vote for particular liquidity allocations.
⠀
This can generate additional economic rewards for eligible vote-locked CVX holders.
⠀
However, these incentives are variable.
⠀
They depend on:
⠀
Protocol budgets.
⠀
Gauge competition.
⠀
Voting participation.
⠀
Market conditions.
⠀
And the value of the reward assets.
⠀
Voting incentives should not be treated as guaranteed recurring cash flows.
⠀
10 | THE REAL REVENUE QUESTION
⠀
Convex has measurable fee and revenue activity.
⠀
DefiLlama reports approximately:
⠀
$2.26M in 30-day fees.
⠀
$926K in 30-day revenue.
⠀
And $881K in 30-day holders revenue.
⠀
But these categories must be interpreted carefully.
⠀
Reported fees include rewards and economic flows associated with the protocol's activities.
⠀
Reported holders revenue includes rewards directed to several eligible staking and locking arrangements.
⠀
It does not mean that every circulating CVX token receives a proportional cash payment.
⠀
Investors must examine actual distributions before estimating tokenholder yield.
⠀
11 | THE VALUATION MULTIPLES
⠀
Using a market capitalization of approximately $160.8M:
⠀
Market Cap / TVL: ~0.33x.
⠀
Annualized 30D Revenue: ~$11.1M.
⠀
Market Cap / Annualized Revenue: ~14.5x.
⠀
These calculations provide a starting point.
⠀
They are not conventional equity valuation multiples.
⠀
TVL represents assets deposited into the protocol, not assets owned by CVX holders.
⠀
And protocol revenue does not automatically belong to every tokenholder.
⠀
The multiple is meaningful only when the underlying revenue definition is understood.
⠀
12 | THE TOKEN SUPPLY STRUCTURE
⠀
CVX has a maximum supply of 100 million tokens.
⠀
Approximately 93.2 million are reported circulating by CoinGecko.
⠀
This represents roughly 93% of maximum supply.
⠀
The original allocation included:
⠀
50% for Curve liquidity provider rewards.
⠀
25% for liquidity mining.
⠀
10% for the team.
⠀
9.7% for the treasury.
⠀
3.3% for investors.
⠀
And 2% for designated veCRV-related allocations.
⠀
The remaining supply difference is relatively limited.
⠀
But investors should still monitor ongoing emissions and liquid supply.
⠀
13 | THE SMART CONTRACT RISK
⠀
Convex operates through smart contracts interacting with other DeFi protocols.
⠀
This introduces multiple layers of technical exposure.
⠀
Potential risks include:
⠀
Smart contract vulnerabilities.
⠀
Underlying protocol exploits.
⠀
Oracle or pricing failures.
⠀
Liquidity disruptions.
⠀
Governance attacks.
⠀
And unexpected reward-token depegging.
⠀
A long operating history is valuable.
⠀
But it does not eliminate systemic DeFi risk.
⠀
14 | THE COMPETITIVE LANDSCAPE
⠀
Convex competes with:
⠀
• Direct Curve participation
• Alternative yield optimizers

Governance incentives strengthen.

Under this scenario, CVX could benefit from renewed demand for DeFi governance and yield infrastructure.

text:
neo:native  — THE FORGOTTEN ETHEREUM RIVAL
⠀
A blockchain once called the Chinese Ethereum.
⠀
A fixed supply of 100 MILLION NEO.
⠀
A dual-token economy that rewards holders with GAS.
⠀
And an EVM-compatible expansion through Neo X.
⠀
But here's the contradiction.
⠀
NEO once traded near $200.
⠀
Today, it trades around $1.76.
⠀
Its market capitalization is approximately $124 million.
⠀
And its original chain has less than $1 million in tracked DeFi TVL.
⠀
Is neo:native one of the most overlooked Layer 1 recovery opportunities?
⠀
Or is the market correctly discounting a blockchain that has struggled to attract meaningful economic activity?
⠀
Let's examine the fundamentals.
⠀
01 | WHAT IS NEO?
⠀
Neo is an established Layer 1 blockchain designed for digital assets, smart contracts, and decentralized applications.
⠀
Originally known as Antshares, the project became one of the most recognizable blockchain platforms during the 2017–2018 market cycle.
⠀
Its infrastructure includes:
⠀
• Neo N3
• Smart contracts
• On-chain governance
• GAS rewards
• Neo X
• NeoFS storage
• Native oracle infrastructure
⠀
Neo's original vision focused on building a smart economy.
⠀
But a strong technological vision does not guarantee ecosystem adoption.
⠀
02 | THE NUMBERS THAT MATTER
⠀
NEO Price: ~$1.76
⠀
Market Cap: ~$124.4M
⠀
Fully Diluted Valuation: ~$176.4M
⠀
Circulating Supply: ~70.53M NEO
⠀
Total Supply: 100M NEO
⠀
Circulating Ratio: ~70.5%
⠀
24H Trading Volume: ~$2.45M
⠀
Historical ATH: ~$198.38
⠀
Neo DeFi TVL: ~$908K
⠀
Neo DEX Volume (24H): ~$2K
⠀
The market data reflects the November 12, 2026 snapshot.
⠀
The DeFi metrics are from November 11.
⠀
The most important contradiction?
⠀
A blockchain valued above $100 million.
⠀
Yet less than $1 million in tracked DeFi liquidity on its original chain.
⠀
03 | THE NEO N3 ARCHITECTURE
⠀
Neo N3 represents a major evolution of the original blockchain.
⠀
Its architecture supports smart contracts, native services, and governance functionality.
⠀
Important features include:
⠀
NeoVM.
⠀
Native oracle services.
⠀
NeoFS integration.
⠀
Digital identity infrastructure.
⠀
And on-chain governance.
⠀
These features provide a broad technical foundation.
⠀
But infrastructure is only valuable when developers and users adopt it.
⠀
The critical question is whether Neo N3 can attract sustained application activity.
⠀
04 | THE DUAL-TOKEN MODEL
⠀
Neo uses two native tokens.
⠀
NEO is the governance token.
⠀
GAS is the network utility token.
⠀
NEO holders can participate in governance and receive GAS according to the network's distribution rules.
⠀
GAS is used for transaction fees, smart contract execution, and other network operations.
⠀
This separates governance from transaction payments.
⠀
But it also creates an important investment distinction.
⠀
Growth in network activity may increase demand for GAS more directly than demand for NEO.
⠀
NEO's investment thesis depends partly on the value of its governance rights and GAS distributions.
⠀
05 | THE GAS REWARD ECONOMY
⠀
NEO holders can receive GAS through the network's reward mechanism.
⠀
Voting participation can significantly affect the amount received.
⠀
The protocol's documented initial allocation distributes generated GAS among NEO holders, governance voters, and committee participants.
⠀
But GAS rewards are not the same as corporate dividends.
⠀
GAS is generated through the network's token economy.
⠀
Its market value depends on supply, network demand, and trading conditions.
⠀
Investors should evaluate:
⠀
GAS rewards per NEO.
⠀
GAS market price.
⠀
Voting participation.
⠀
And the sustainability of the reward structure.
⠀
Nominal token rewards do not guarantee positive dollar-denominated returns.
⠀
06 | THE SUPPLY STRUCTURE
⠀
NEO has a fixed total supply of 100 million tokens.
⠀
Approximately 70.53 million are classified as circulating.
⠀
That leaves a meaningful difference between circulating supply and total supply.
⠀
NEO itself is not newly mined through a conventional inflationary issuance schedule.
⠀
However, investors must still understand the ownership and liquidity of tokens outside reported circulation.
⠀
The relevant questions are:
⠀
Who controls the remaining supply?
⠀
What restrictions apply?
⠀
And could additional tokens enter the liquid market?
⠀
A fixed total supply does not eliminate distribution-related selling pressure.
⠀
07 | THE NEO X EXPANSION
⠀
Neo X is an EVM-compatible sidechain designed to connect Neo's ecosystem with Ethereum-compatible tooling.
⠀
This matters because EVM compatibility can reduce development friction.
⠀
Developers can potentially reuse familiar tools and smart contract frameworks.
⠀
Neo X also emphasizes its consensus design and resistance to harmful MEV practices.
⠀
But compatibility alone is not a competitive advantage.
⠀
The market already includes numerous EVM-compatible networks.
⠀
Neo X must compete on liquidity, developer incentives, user experience, and application demand.
⠀
The most important metric is real adoption after launch.
⠀
08 | THE DEFI ADOPTION PROBLEM
⠀
This is the most concerning part of the investment thesis.
⠀
DefiLlama reports approximately $908,000 in DeFi TVL on Neo's original chain.
⠀
Reported 24-hour DEX volume is approximately $2,000.
⠀
These figures indicate extremely limited tracked DeFi activity.
⠀
They do not represent every possible economic activity across the wider Neo ecosystem.
⠀
Neo X should be evaluated separately.
⠀
But the numbers still raise a serious question.
⠀
Why has a long-established smart contract blockchain failed to retain deeper DeFi liquidity?
⠀
Technology without liquidity struggles to attract users.
⠀
And applications without users struggle to attract developers.
⠀
09 | THE FLAMINGO ECOSYSTEM
⠀
Flamingo is one of Neo's recognizable DeFi applications.
⠀
It provides decentralized trading and related financial functionality.
⠀
However, its tracked liquidity and trading activity remain small compared with major DeFi ecosystems.
⠀
This creates challenges for:
⠀
Trading depth.
⠀
Capital efficiency.
⠀
Slippage.
⠀
User acquisition.
⠀
And sustainable protocol revenue.
⠀
A functioning DEX demonstrates infrastructure.
⠀
But substantial liquidity is necessary for competitive financial markets.
⠀
10 | THE REVENUE QUESTION
⠀
Neo's ecosystem economics require careful interpretation.
⠀
Network transaction fees are paid in GAS.
⠀
GAS generation provides rewards to eligible participants.
⠀
And certain system fees are burned.
⠀
These mechanisms influence the GAS economy.
⠀
But they do not automatically create direct cash flows for NEO holders.
⠀
The relevant indicators include:
⠀
Network transactions.
⠀
GAS fees.
⠀
GAS burned.
⠀
GAS generated.
⠀
Application revenue.
⠀
And the value of GAS distributed to NEO holders.
⠀
A token can offer rewards while the underlying ecosystem generates little external revenue.
⠀
11 | THE GOVERNANCE MODEL
⠀
NEO holders participate in governance through voting.
⠀
Governance influences committee selection and network parameters.
⠀
The system is built around delegated Byzantine Fault Tolerance.
⠀
This can support efficient transaction finality.
⠀
But governance concentration remains an important risk.
⠀
Investors should monitor:
⠀
Voting participation.
⠀
Committee composition.
⠀
Validator concentration.
⠀
And governance decision-making.
⠀
A technically efficient consensus system is not automatically maximally decentralized.
⠀
12 | THE CHINA NARRATIVE
⠀
NEO became widely known as the Chinese Ethereum.
⠀
That historical identity helped attract investor attention during earlier market cycles.
⠀
But investors should not confuse a China-linked narrative with official government endorsement.
⠀
Nor should they assume that regulatory developments in China will directly benefit NEO.
⠀
The relevant question is whether Neo can attract developers, capital, and users regardless of its historical branding.
⠀
A narrative can generate speculative demand.
⠀
But sustainable valuation requires measurable economic activity.
⠀
13 | THE COMPETITIVE LANDSCAPE
⠀
NEO competes with:
⠀
• Ethereum
• Solana
• BNB Chain
• Avalanche
• Sui
• Other EVM-compatible networks
⠀
Its strengths include a long operating history, a fixed NEO supply, and the GAS reward mechanism.
⠀
But competitors possess substantially larger developer ecosystems, liquidity pools, and user networks.
⠀
Neo X may improve compatibility.
⠀
It does not automatically solve the distribution problem.
⠀
The central challenge is rebuilding network effects.
⠀
14 | THE HISTORICAL PRICE TRAP
⠀
NEO reached an all-time high near $198.
⠀
At approximately $1.76, it trades more than 99% below that peak.
⠀
This may appear attractive to investors searching for deeply discounted assets.
⠀
But a 99% drawdown is not evidence of undervaluation.
⠀
A token can remain far below its previous high when market structure, competition, and demand change.
⠀
The important question is not whether NEO can revisit its historical peak.
⠀
It's whether its current ecosystem can justify a higher valuation.
⠀
15 | THE VALUATION FRAMEWORK
⠀
Using NEO's fixed total supply of 100 million tokens:
⠀
$2 NEO implies $200M FDV.
⠀
$5 implies $500M.
⠀
$10 implies $1B.
⠀
$20 implies $2B.
⠀
$50 implies $5B.
⠀
$100 implies $10B.
⠀
These are illustrative valuations, not price targets.
⠀
A $10 NEO price would imply a fully diluted valuation of $1 billion.
⠀
That would require a major improvement in market expectations compared with the current valuation.
⠀
Without meaningful growth in users, liquidity, and economic activity, a sustained revaluation would be difficult to justify fundamentally.
⠀
16 | THE BULL CASE
⠀
NEO could benefit if:
⠀
Neo X attracts EVM developers.
⠀
New applications bring liquidity.
⠀
DeFi TVL recovers.
⠀
GAS demand increases.
⠀
Governance participation strengthens.
⠀
And the market rotates toward established Layer 1 assets.
⠀
Under this scenario, NEO could experience renewed investor interest.
⠀
But the strongest confirmation would come from measurable ecosystem growth.
⠀
Not simply a price breakout.
⠀
17 | THE BEAR CASE
⠀
The bearish scenario is equally important.
⠀
Neo N3 continues losing relevance.
⠀
Neo X fails to attract meaningful adoption.
⠀
DeFi liquidity remains extremely limited.
⠀
Developers prioritize larger ecosystems.
⠀
GAS rewards fail to compensate for NEO price weakness.
⠀
And historical brand recognition becomes less relevant.
⠀
Under this scenario, NEO could remain a technically functioning blockchain with limited economic demand.
⠀
18 | THE FINAL VERDICT
⠀
NEO has several genuine strengths.
⠀
A fixed 100 million token supply.
⠀
A long operating history.
⠀
A functioning governance system.
⠀
A dual-token economy.
⠀
And EVM expansion through Neo X.
⠀
But here's the contradiction.
⠀
A blockchain once valued as a major Ethereum competitor.
⠀
An established technical infrastructure.
⠀
And a token trading more than 99% below its historical peak.
⠀
Yet less than $1 million in tracked DeFi TVL on its original chain.
⠀
The next major catalyst isn't simply another roadmap announcement.
⠀
It's evidence that Neo can rebuild real economic activity.
⠀
Technology demonstrates capability.
⠀
GAS rewards demonstrate token utility.
⠀
Neo X demonstrates expansion.
⠀
But liquidity, developers, and paying users determine long-term relevance.
⠀
The market isn't asking whether NEO can still operate.
⠀
It's asking whether NEO can become economically important again.
⠀
Bookmark this analysis before the next legacy Layer 1 rotation.
⠀
Which has the strongest comeback potential?
⠀
neo:native, $EOS, or tezos:native?
⠀
And can Neo X bring meaningful adoption back to the Neo ecosystem?
⠀

thorchain:native  — THE CROSS-CHAIN DEFI INFRASTRUCTURE BET
⠀
A $195 MILLION cryptocurrency.
⠀
Approximately $16.9 MILLION in annual protocol fees.
⠀
A decentralized exchange that enables native Bitcoin swaps.
⠀
And a token trading more than 97% below its all-time high.
⠀
But here's the contradiction.
⠀
THORChain operates real infrastructure with measurable trading demand.
⠀
RUNE is required for liquidity, settlement, and network security.
⠀
Yet the ecosystem has also experienced a major debt crisis, controversial restructuring, and significant economic changes.
⠀
Is thorchain:native one of the most overlooked revenue-generating DeFi assets?
⠀
Or is the market correctly discounting its operational and financial risks?
⠀
Let's examine the fundamentals.
⠀
01 | WHAT IS THORCHAIN?
⠀
THORChain is a decentralized cross-chain liquidity protocol.
⠀
Its primary purpose is to enable swaps between native blockchain assets without relying on conventional wrapped-token bridges.
⠀
Its infrastructure supports:
⠀
• Native BTC swaps
• ETH and other major assets
• Cross-chain liquidity pools
• Decentralized settlement
• Validator security
• Wallet and exchange integrations
• Protocol-owned liquidity
⠀
The objective is to provide decentralized liquidity across otherwise disconnected blockchain networks.
⠀
But technological usefulness does not automatically make RUNE undervalued.
⠀
02 | THE NUMBERS THAT MATTER
⠀
November 12, 2026 snapshot:
⠀
RUNE Price: ~$0.592
Market Cap: ~$195M
FDV: ~$209M
Circulating Supply: ~329.15M RUNE
Total Supply: ~353.85M RUNE
24H Reported Trading Volume: ~$181M
All-Time High: ~$20.87
Decline From ATH: ~97.2%
⠀
THORCHAIN FUNDAMENTALS:
⠀
12M Protocol Fees: ~$16.9M
Reported TVL: ~$61.2M
Active Node Bond: ~100M RUNE
Active Nodes: ~111
Cumulative RUNE Burned: ~2.18M
⠀
The token's market capitalization is relatively small compared with its historical role in cross-chain DeFi.
⠀
But current revenue, liquidity, and security conditions matter more than historical reputation.
⠀
03 | THE NATIVE SWAP ADVANTAGE
⠀
Most blockchains operate independently.
⠀
Moving assets between networks often requires bridges, wrapped tokens, or centralized intermediaries.
⠀
THORChain offers a different approach.
⠀
Users can exchange supported native assets through decentralized liquidity pools.
⠀
This creates a potentially valuable service.
⠀
Especially for users who want to swap Bitcoin without relying on a centralized exchange.
⠀
But native settlement does not eliminate every security risk.
⠀
Validator coordination, protocol implementation, liquidity management, and cross-chain integrations remain important attack surfaces.
⠀
04 | WHY RUNE MATTERS
⠀
RUNE is central to THORChain's architecture.
⠀
Its major functions include:
⠀
Liquidity settlement.
⠀
Validator bonding.
⠀
Network gas.
⠀
Economic incentives.
⠀
And protocol security.
⠀
THORChain liquidity pools pair supported assets with RUNE.
⠀
This creates a structural relationship between pool liquidity and demand for the native token.
⠀
Unlike a token used only for governance voting, RUNE participates directly in the protocol's operating model.
⠀
That is one of its strongest fundamental advantages.
⠀
05 | THE LIQUIDITY MULTIPLIER
⠀
THORChain's original tokenomics describe a relationship between non-RUNE liquidity and RUNE required for pools and network security.
⠀
The historical model targeted:
⠀
$1 of RUNE liquidity for every $1 of non-RUNE pool assets.
⠀
Plus approximately $2 of bonded RUNE for security.
⠀
This produced the well-known 3:1 economic framework.
⠀
But investors should not treat this as an immutable valuation formula.
⠀
Bonding requirements, protocol-owned liquidity, pool composition, and incentive parameters can change.
⠀
The relevant measure is actual RUNE locked in pools and validator bonds.
⠀
Not a theoretical price multiplier.
⠀
06 | THE REAL REVENUE ADVANTAGE
⠀
THORChain's official dashboard reports approximately $16.9 million in protocol fees over the last 12 months.
⠀
That is meaningful compared with many Layer 1 projects that generate very little economic activity.
⠀
But fees are not the same as profit.
⠀
And protocol revenue is not equivalent to cash distributed to every RUNE holder.
⠀
The network uses fees to support several economic functions.
⠀
The correct analysis must follow where those fees actually go.
⠀
07 | THE FEE DISTRIBUTION MODEL
⠀
THORChain's published allocation model currently describes:
⠀
1% — RUNE burns
⠀
5% — Marketing
⠀
5% — Developers
⠀
10% — TCY holders
⠀
20% — Protocol-owned liquidity
⠀
59% — Nodes and liquidity pools
⠀
This creates several distinct beneficiaries.
⠀
The entire fee stream does not belong to RUNE holders.
⠀
Some revenue supports security.
⠀
Some supports liquidity.
⠀
Some supports development.
⠀
And a portion is allocated to creditors through TCY.
⠀
The distribution structure is essential when evaluating RUNE.
⠀
08 | THE THORFI DEBT CRISIS
⠀
THORChain experienced a major financial crisis in early 2025 involving its THORFi lending and savings products.
⠀
The restructuring addressed approximately $210 million in outstanding obligations.
⠀
Affected creditors received TCY tokens as part of the resolution.
⠀
This was a significant event.
⠀
It demonstrated that decentralized infrastructure can still develop serious balance-sheet and liquidity problems.
⠀
The protocol continued operating.
⠀
But the restructuring changed how future economic value is distributed.
⠀
A functioning protocol is not necessarily a financially risk-free protocol.
⠀
09 | THE TCY TOKEN
⠀
TCY was introduced as part of THORChain's debt restructuring.
⠀
Its initial allocation was designed around approximately 210 million tokens.
⠀
The model directs 10% of protocol income toward TCY holders.
⠀
This matters because TCY and RUNE have different economic functions.
⠀
RUNE is the network's settlement and security asset.
⠀
TCY represents a specific revenue-sharing arrangement created through restructuring.
⠀
Investors should not confuse the two.
⠀
A growing protocol can benefit multiple economic stakeholders without distributing all gains to RUNE holders.
⠀
10 | THE TOKEN SUPPLY ADVANTAGE
⠀
THORChain reports approximately 353.85 million RUNE in total supply.
⠀
Around 329.15 million are circulating according to CoinGecko.
⠀
The project's official tokenomics state that the final scheduled RUNE unlock occurred in 2023.
⠀
It also states that block-reward inflation has ended.
⠀
This reduces the conventional vesting pressure associated with many newer crypto projects.
⠀
However, reported circulating supply and the project's own reserve classifications differ.
⠀
Those categories should be reconciled rather than treated as identical.
⠀
A mature supply structure is an advantage.
⠀
But it does not eliminate market selling pressure.
⠀
11 | THE RUNE BURN MECHANISM
⠀
THORChain allocates approximately 1% of network fees toward RUNE burns.
⠀
The official dashboard reports more than 2.18 million RUNE burned cumulatively.
⠀
Burns can permanently reduce supply.
⠀
But their impact depends on the amount destroyed relative to outstanding supply.
⠀
Against roughly 354 million total RUNE, 2.18 million represents approximately 0.62%.
⠀
That is meaningful as a mechanism.
⠀
But it is not sufficient by itself to establish a strong deflationary investment thesis.
⠀
Future burns depend on actual network activity and fee generation.
⠀
12 | THE VALIDATOR SECURITY MODEL
⠀
THORChain relies on node operators that bond RUNE to secure the network.
⠀
The network explorer recently reported approximately 100 million RUNE in active node bonds.
⠀
This creates substantial economic demand for bonded RUNE.
⠀
But security must be evaluated through more than the nominal value of bonds.
⠀
Important variables include:
⠀
Bond concentration.
⠀
Validator participation.
⠀
Node rotation.
⠀
Economic incentives.
⠀
And the value of assets held in liquidity pools.
⠀
A large bonded supply can support network security.
⠀
But security assumptions can weaken if incentives become misaligned.
⠀
13 | THE LIQUIDITY QUESTION
⠀
CoinGecko reports approximately $61.2 million in THORChain TVL.
⠀
This is materially smaller than the liquidity scale seen during stronger market periods.
⠀
But THORChain should not be evaluated only through TVL.
⠀
Its business depends heavily on trading activity and liquidity efficiency.
⠀
A smaller pool can still process meaningful volume.
⠀
However, reduced liquidity can increase slippage and limit the size of trades the network can execute competitively.
⠀
The strongest indicators are:
⠀
Cross-chain swap volume.
⠀
Trading fees.
⠀
Liquidity depth.
⠀
Repeat users.
⠀
And sustainable revenue.
⠀
14 | THE SECURITY AND COMPLIANCE RISK
⠀
Permissionless cross-chain infrastructure can attract legitimate users seeking decentralized settlement.
⠀
But it can also be used to move illicit funds.
⠀
THORChain has faced scrutiny over its role in processing assets connected to major cryptocurrency thefts.
⠀
This creates potential reputational and regulatory risks.
⠀
Investors should distinguish between the protocol's technical ability to process transactions and the legal responsibilities of identifiable operators or service providers.
⠀
A decentralized architecture does not eliminate compliance concerns.
⠀
These risks can influence integrations, liquidity providers, and institutional participation.
⠀
15 | THE COMPETITIVE CHALLENGE
⠀
THORChain competes with:
⠀
• Centralized exchanges
• Cross-chain bridges
• Chain abstraction protocols
• Intent-based trading systems

3. DEFENCE, SPACE & AUTONOMY — $ONDS, $LUNR, $SPCE

I'll be watching payment volumes, take rates, margins and free cash flow.
For StoneCo and Figure, the focus is sustainable growth, operating leverage and credit or funding risks where applicable.

I'm still bullish on the long-term AI infrastructure opportunity, particularly companies building the capacity needed to support sustained growth in AI workloads.
Today's UK data adds another dimension. Stronger manufacturing and business investment are encouraging, but the widening trade deficit and weakness in construction suggest the recovery remains uneven.
Meanwhile, the market is becoming increasingly sensitive to financing costs, deployment timelines and the returns generated by each additional dollar of capital expenditure.
Nebius is a particularly important test of that investment thesis today.
Applied Materials and Cisco will also help show whether AI infrastructure demand continues to support the wider semiconductor equipment and networking ecosystem.
WHAT MATTERS NEXT
AI contracts → Power capacity → GPU deployment → Utilisation → Revenue

Semiconductor investment → Equipment demand → Advanced packaging → AI compute capacity
UK growth → Inflation expectations → Bank of England policy → Gilt yields
U.S. labour market → Fed expectations → Treasury yields → Financing costs → Shareholder returns
The AI buildout is still a major long-term opportunity. What matters increasingly is which companies can turn that opportunity into sustainable cash returns.
That's what I'll be watching today.
